Sheet Metal vs CNC Machining: How to Choose the Right Method for Your Metal Parts Quick Answer: Choose sheet metal for uniform-thickness enclosures, panels, and formed brackets when bends and production volume support lower unit cost. Choose CNC machining for variable wall thickness, precision bores, tight feature relationships, and complex 3D geometry. Use a hybrid design when a formed structure needs precision-machined interfaces. A quote comes back for a bracket, and it's priced as a CNC part — machined from solid aluminum, a few hours of spindle time, a per-part cost that makes sense for ten units but starts looking painful at a thousand. The same bracket, cut and bent from sheet stock, would cost a fraction of that at volume. Nobody made a mistake here; the part just got quoted through the wrong process for its actual requirements. That mismatch — sheet metal work priced and built like a machined part, or vice versa — is one of the more expensive mistakes in early product design, and it's usually avoidable with a clear framework for which process actually fits. The Core Difference Sheet metal fabrication forms a part from flat stock — cutting, bending, and joining thin material into its final shape. CNC machining removes material from a solid block until the final geometry emerges. That distinction — forming versus removing — is what drives almost every practical difference between the two: cost structure, achievable geometry, tolerance, and how each scales with volume. It's also why the two processes don't compete on a level playing field for most parts — once you know which side of "form vs. remove" your part naturally sits on, half the decision is already made before cost even enters the conversation. CNC or Sheet Metal — We Do Both Need CNC and Sheet Metal? We've Got Both JLCCNC does both CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication in-house. Upload your file, get an instant quote. Get Instant Quote Decision Framework Factor Favors Sheet Metal Favors CNC Machining Wall thickness Uniform, thin — typically under 6mm, though this depends on material and forming method Variable thickness, thick sections Geometry Flat panels, bent enclosures, brackets Complex 3D features, pockets, threaded bosses Tolerance ±0.1–0.3mm typical, tighter with secondary operations ±0.01–0.05mm achievable, depending on material and feature size Material waste Low — forming generates minimal scrap Higher — material is cut away as chips Volume economics Cost drops fast with volume, but the rate depends heavily on whether the process is press-brake bending or stamping Cost scales more linearly with volume Prototype cost Can be higher per-unit at very low volume due to setup Often cheaper for true one-offs (no tooling needed) Lead time Faster once in production; batch-dependent Often faster for a single prototype, no setup to plan around Surface finish out of process Generally rougher without secondary finishing, though this varies by material and process Can achieve fine finish directly off the tool The numbers above are typical ranges, not guarantees — actual tolerance and thickness limits depend on the specific material, part size, forming or cutting method, and feature geometry involved. Neither column is "better" in the abstract — the right answer depends entirely on which factors matter for a specific part. How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree The table above tells you what each process is generally good at. This turns that into something you can actually run a part through: Is wall thickness uniform across the part? If yes, sheet metal is still in play. If the part needs varying thickness in different sections, that alone usually rules sheet metal out. Can the geometry be formed by bending, rather than requiring it be cut from solid? A flat pattern that folds into the final shape favors sheet metal. A shape with internal pockets, bosses, or geometry that can't unfold flat needs machining. Does any feature need a precision bore, bearing seat, or tightly toleranced hole relationship? If yes, that feature — and possibly the whole part — needs CNC, even if the rest of the geometry would otherwise suit sheet metal. Where does your volume sit? Low volume with simple geometry often favors CNC (no tooling, no bend planning). Moderate-to-high volume with sheet-metal-compatible geometry usually favors sheet metal. Does the part actually need to be one piece, or could it be a hybrid? If step 3 flagged a precision feature but the rest of the part is sheet-metal-friendly, a hybrid assembly is often cheaper than machining the whole thing. Running an actual part through these five questions in order, rather than defaulting to whichever process a designer is more familiar with, is usually enough to catch a mismatch before it turns into a bad quote. Where Sheet Metal Wins Enclosures, panels, brackets, and chassis with mostly uniform wall thickness are sheet metal's home turf. A sheet metal enclosure that would need a solid block of aluminum hollowed out on a mill costs dramatically more in both material and machine time than the same shape cut flat and folded into a box. At production volume, this gap widens further — sheet metal's low scrap rate and fast cycle time on simple bends make it the clear cost winner for parts that don't need machining's tighter tolerances or 3D complexity. There are design rules that come with this territory, and they're worth knowing before a part gets drawn rather than after it comes back from the shop with a note attached. Holes placed too close to a bend line will distort during forming — a rough rule of thumb is keeping at least 3x the material thickness between a hole's edge and the bend line. Minimum bend radius matters too: pushing a bend tighter than the material can reasonably take leads to cracking on the outer surface, especially with harder alloys. These aren't limitations that make sheet metal a lesser option — they're just the constraints that come with forming instead of removing material, and designing around them from the start avoids a redesign cycle later. Our sheet metal design guidelines go deeper into these bend, hole-spacing, and flange rules if you're drawing a part now. Where CNC Machining Wins Anything needing tight tolerances, threaded holes machined directly into the part, varying wall thickness, or complex 3D features that can't be formed from flat stock belongs in CNC machining. A mounting plate needing precisely located, tightly toleranced holes for a bearing assembly isn't a sheet metal job — the tolerance and feature complexity simply exceed what forming can reliably produce. Deep features have their own limits worth knowing on the machining side. A pocket deeper than roughly four times its diameter starts requiring longer, more flexible tooling, which drives up cycle time and cost, and increases the risk of chatter or tool deflection affecting the finish. It doesn't rule the feature out — it just changes the cost math, and it's another reason "can CNC do it" and "should CNC do it at this price point" are different questions. For true one-off prototypes, machining is also often cheaper in practice, since it needs no tooling investment the way some sheet metal processes — stamping in particular — do. Standard press-brake bending, the default for custom and low-volume sheet metal work, doesn't carry that same tooling penalty; it's cutting and forming operations, not a stamping die, which is why a low-volume bracket cut on a laser and folded on a brake can still compete with machining on price even without any tooling amortized into it. Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Volume matters, but it's not the whole cost story — and treating "sheet metal wins at volume" as the entire rule misses where the actual cost comes from on each side. On the sheet metal side , cost is driven by material utilization (how efficiently the flat pattern nests on the sheet), the number of cuts and bends, whether parts need welding or additional fastening, and any secondary surface finishing. A part with a simple flat pattern and two bends costs very differently from one with a dozen tabs, slots, and a welded seam — even at the same volume and material. On the CNC side , cost tracks the size of the starting stock, how much material has to be removed to reach final geometry, how many times the part needs to be re-fixtured to reach all its features, tooling wear on harder materials, and how tightly toleranced features need inspecting after the cut. A part that looks simple but needs machining from six sides costs more than its footprint suggests, regardless of order quantity. This is also where the sheet metal tooling question matters. Laser cutting and press-brake bending — the default route for prototypes and low-to-moderate volume custom sheet metal — carry no tooling cost; you're paying for cutting and setup time per batch. Stamping, by contrast, requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront cost that only pays off once volume is high enough to amortize it across thousands of parts. Comparing a stamped-part cost curve to a CNC part is a different conversation than comparing a laser-cut-and-bent part to a CNC part, and conflating the two is a common source of quotes that don't match expectations. Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Some features have a real answer on which process they need, and it's worth being direct about which ones: bearing bores, features requiring tight coaxiality between two holes, precisely located dowel or locating pin holes, and complex internal cavities are CNC territory. Sheet metal forming doesn't hold that level of geometric precision, and no amount of secondary finishing changes that. But it's a mistake to jump straight to "this part needs a thread, so it needs CNC." Sheet metal has its own ways of handling fasteners and threaded connections without machining the whole part: bent tabs with clearance holes, PEM self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet, riveted nuts, or welded studs all add threaded or fastening points to a sheet metal part without requiring the part itself be machined. The real question isn't "does this need a thread" — it's "does this need a machined thread in solid material, or would a pressed-in fastener do the job." Most bracket and enclosure fastening needs fall into the second category. Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal This is often the highest-value move in the whole decision, and it's the one that's easy to miss when a part starts life as a CNC drawing and never gets reconsidered. If a part is currently machined but doesn't actually need machining's precision everywhere, redesigning it around sheet metal can cut cost meaningfully at volume. A few principles that tend to work: Unify wall thickness. A machined part with varying wall thickness for structural reasons can often be redesigned around a single uniform thickness plus added ribs or folded flanges for stiffness, opening the door to sheet metal. Replace pocketed/hollowed sections with a folded shell. A block that's mostly hollowed out to save weight is, functionally, often just an enclosure — which is exactly what sheet metal is good at forming instead of removing material to create. Use flanges and fasteners instead of solid thick walls. Where a machined part relies on thick material for mounting strength, a folded flange with the right fastener often does the same structural job at a fraction of the material cost. Keep precision interfaces as small, separate CNC parts. The redesign doesn't have to eliminate machining entirely — isolating the one feature that genuinely needs tight tolerance into a small machined insert, bolted or riveted into a sheet metal shell, usually costs less than machining the whole part just to get that one feature right. One Hybrid Assembly Example Plenty of real products aren't a clean either/or. A sheet metal chassis provides the lightweight, cost-effective structural shell, while CNC-machined brackets or mounting plates handle the specific spots that need tight tolerances a formed part can't hold — bolted or riveted into the sheet metal structure. A common version of this: a sheet-metal chassis with a CNC-machined bearing bracket bolted into it. The chassis handles the overall shape, mounting points, and structural panel work — all things sheet metal does well and cheaply at volume. The bearing bracket needs a precisely bored, tightly toleranced hole to seat a bearing correctly, which sheet metal forming can't reliably hold. Rather than machining the entire chassis to get that one bore right, the bore lives on a small dedicated machined part, and the two interfaces — chassis mounting holes and bracket mounting holes — are designed to align during assembly. This hybrid approach is common enough in electronics and equipment housings that it's worth considering from the start of a design, rather than defaulting to one process and forcing every feature to fit it. It's also one of the more practical reasons to source both processes from the same shop — fewer handoffs, fewer tolerance mismatches between the two parts when they're meant to bolt together. Our enclosure design guide goes deeper into this specific decision for enclosure design — covering the same choice this article addresses, but focused on the practical challenges of enclosure geometry, internal component fit, and assembly. Material Considerations The two processes don't just differ in how they shape metal — they differ in which metals are practical to work with, and that's often the deciding factor before cost or geometry even get discussed. Aluminum 5052 forms well and is a workhorse for sheet metal enclosures, but it's a softer alloy that machines less cleanly at tight tolerances than harder grades. Aluminum 6061 is the opposite pattern: it machines cleanly and holds tolerance well on a CNC part, but its formability is more limited — tight bend radii in 6061 are more prone to cracking than in 5052. 304 and 201 stainless steel both fabricate well as sheet metal for enclosures and structural panels, but on the machining side stainless work-hardens as it's cut, which means slower feeds, more tool wear, and a costlier part than the same geometry in aluminum or steel. Cold rolled steel is a common, economical choice for sheet metal work and machines acceptably too, which is part of why it shows up so often in both processes for general-purpose brackets and housings. If a design is locked into a specific alloy for strength, corrosion resistance, or cost reasons, it's worth checking that alloy's behavior in the process you're leaning toward before finalizing — a great geometry choice can still get expensive if the material fights the process. See our guide to sheet metal material types for a fuller breakdown by alloy. The Real Cost Curve The mismatch described at the top of this article — a bracket quoted as CNC when sheet metal would've been dramatically cheaper at volume — happens because the two processes' cost curves cross at different points depending on the part. At very low volume (a handful of prototypes), the two are often close, sometimes with machining even edging ahead since sheet metal's setup costs don't amortize yet. As volume grows, sheet metal's per-part cost typically drops well below machining's for parts within its geometric capability — since machining cost stays tied to cutting time and material removed no matter how many parts you order, while sheet metal's setup cost gets spread across a growing batch. Exactly where that crossover happens shifts with the factors above; a simple two-bend bracket crosses over earlier than a part needing several welds and a finish operation. Push volume high enough and the gap widens further for simple flat-and-bend geometries, though a part with genuinely complex 3D features may never cross over — sheet metal simply can't produce it at any volume, which makes the "geometry first, cost second" ordering of this decision worth sticking to. See our breakdown of CNC machining costs for more on how machining cost is actually built up. Sheet Metal vs CNC Machining: How to Choose the Right Method for Your Metal Parts Quick Answer: Choose sheet metal for uniform-thickness enclosures, panels, and formed brackets when bends and production volume support lower unit cost. Choose CNC machining for variable wall thickness, precision bores, tight feature relationships, and complex 3D geometry. Use a hybrid design when a formed structure needs precision-machined interfaces. A quote comes back for a bracket, and it's priced as a CNC part — machined from solid aluminum, a few hours of spindle time, a per-part cost that makes sense for ten units but starts looking painful at a thousand. The same bracket, cut and bent from sheet stock, would cost a fraction of that at volume. Nobody made a mistake here; the part just got quoted through the wrong process for its actual requirements. That mismatch — sheet metal work priced and built like a machined part, or vice versa — is one of the more expensive mistakes in early product design, and it's usually avoidable with a clear framework for which process actually fits. The Core Difference Sheet metal fabrication forms a part from flat stock — cutting, bending, and joining thin material into its final shape. CNC machining removes material from a solid block until the final geometry emerges. That distinction — forming versus removing — is what drives almost every practical difference between the two: cost structure, achievable geometry, tolerance, and how each scales with volume. It's also why the two processes don't compete on a level playing field for most parts — once you know which side of "form vs. remove" your part naturally sits on, half the decision is already made before cost even enters the conversation. Neither column is "better" in the abstract — the right answer depends entirely on which factors matter for a specific part. How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree The table above tells you what each process is generally good at. This turns that into something you can actually run a part through: Is wall thickness uniform across the part? If yes, sheet metal is still in play. If the part needs varying thickness in different sections, that alone usually rules sheet metal out. Can the geometry be formed by bending, rather than requiring it be cut from solid? A flat pattern that folds into the final shape favors sheet metal. A shape with internal pockets, bosses, or geometry that can't unfold flat needs machining. Does any feature need a precision bore, bearing seat, or tightly toleranced hole relationship? If yes, that feature — and possibly the whole part — needs CNC, even if the rest of the geometry would otherwise suit sheet metal. Where does your volume sit? Low volume with simple geometry often favors CNC (no tooling, no bend planning). Moderate-to-high volume with sheet-metal-compatible geometry usually favors sheet metal. Does the part actually need to be one piece, or could it be a hybrid? If step 3 flagged a precision feature but the rest of the part is sheet-metal-friendly, a hybrid assembly is often cheaper than machining the whole thing. Running an actual part through these five questions in order, rather than defaulting to whichever process a designer is more familiar with, is usually enough to catch a mismatch before it turns into a bad quote. Where Sheet Metal Wins Enclosures, panels, brackets, and chassis with mostly uniform wall thickness are sheet metal's home turf. A sheet metal enclosure that would need a solid block of aluminum hollowed out on a mill costs dramatically more in both material and machine time than the same shape cut flat and folded into a box. At production volume, this gap widens further — sheet metal's low scrap rate and fast cycle time on simple bends make it the clear cost winner for parts that don't need machining's tighter tolerances or 3D complexity. There are design rules that come with this territory, and they're worth knowing before a part gets drawn rather than after it comes back from the shop with a note attached. Holes placed too close to a bend line will distort during forming — a rough rule of thumb is keeping at least 3x the material thickness between a hole's edge and the bend line. Minimum bend radius matters too: pushing a bend tighter than the material can reasonably take leads to cracking on the outer surface, especially with harder alloys. These aren't limitations that make sheet metal a lesser option — they're just the constraints that come with forming instead of removing material, and designing around them from the start avoids a redesign cycle later. Our sheet metal design guidelines go deeper into these bend, hole-spacing, and flange rules if you're drawing a part now. Where CNC Machining Wins Anything needing tight tolerances, threaded holes machined directly into the part, varying wall thickness, or complex 3D features that can't be formed from flat stock belongs in CNC machining. A mounting plate needing precisely located, tightly toleranced holes for a bearing assembly isn't a sheet metal job — the tolerance and feature complexity simply exceed what forming can reliably produce. Deep features have their own limits worth knowing on the machining side. A pocket deeper than roughly four times its diameter starts requiring longer, more flexible tooling, which drives up cycle time and cost, and increases the risk of chatter or tool deflection affecting the finish. It doesn't rule the feature out — it just changes the cost math, and it's another reason "can CNC do it" and "should CNC do it at this price point" are different questions. For true one-off prototypes, machining is also often cheaper in practice, since it needs no tooling investment the way some sheet metal processes — stamping in particular — do. Standard press-brake bending, the default for custom and low-volume sheet metal work, doesn't carry that same tooling penalty; it's cutting and forming operations, not a stamping die, which is why a low-volume bracket cut on a laser and folded on a brake can still compete with machining on price even without any tooling amortized into it. Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Volume matters, but it's not the whole cost story — and treating "sheet metal wins at volume" as the entire rule misses where the actual cost comes from on each side. On the sheet metal side , cost is driven by material utilization (how efficiently the flat pattern nests on the sheet), the number of cuts and bends, whether parts need welding or additional fastening, and any secondary surface finishing. A part with a simple flat pattern and two bends costs very differently from one with a dozen tabs, slots, and a welded seam — even at the same volume and material. On the CNC side , cost tracks the size of the starting stock, how much material has to be removed to reach final geometry, how many times the part needs to be re-fixtured to reach all its features, tooling wear on harder materials, and how tightly toleranced features need inspecting after the cut. A part that looks simple but needs machining from six sides costs more than its footprint suggests, regardless of order quantity. This is also where the sheet metal tooling question matters. Laser cutting and press-brake bending — the default route for prototypes and low-to-moderate volume custom sheet metal — carry no tooling cost; you're paying for cutting and setup time per batch. Stamping, by contrast, requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront cost that only pays off once volume is high enough to amortize it across thousands of parts. Comparing a stamped-part cost curve to a CNC part is a different conversation than comparing a laser-cut-and-bent part to a CNC part, and conflating the two is a common source of quotes that don't match expectations. Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Some features have a real answer on which process they need, and it's worth being direct about which ones: bearing bores, features requiring tight coaxiality between two holes, precisely located dowel or locating pin holes, and complex internal cavities are CNC territory. Sheet metal forming doesn't hold that level of geometric precision, and no amount of secondary finishing changes that. But it's a mistake to jump straight to "this part needs a thread, so it needs CNC." Sheet metal has its own ways of handling fasteners and threaded connections without machining the whole part: bent tabs with clearance holes, PEM self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet, riveted nuts, or welded studs all add threaded or fastening points to a sheet metal part without requiring the part itself be machined. The real question isn't "does this need a thread" — it's "does this need a machined thread in solid material, or would a pressed-in fastener do the job." Most bracket and enclosure fastening needs fall into the second category. Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal This is often the highest-value move in the whole decision, and it's the one that's easy to miss when a part starts life as a CNC drawing and never gets reconsidered. If a part is currently machined but doesn't actually need machining's precision everywhere, redesigning it around sheet metal can cut cost meaningfully at volume. A few principles that tend to work: Unify wall thickness. A machined part with varying wall thickness for structural reasons can often be redesigned around a single uniform thickness plus added ribs or folded flanges for stiffness, opening the door to sheet metal. Replace pocketed/hollowed sections with a folded shell. A block that's mostly hollowed out to save weight is, functionally, often just an enclosure — which is exactly what sheet metal is good at forming instead of removing material to create. Use flanges and fasteners instead of solid thick walls. Where a machined part relies on thick material for mounting strength, a folded flange with the right fastener often does the same structural job at a fraction of the material cost. Keep precision interfaces as small, separate CNC parts. The redesign doesn't have to eliminate machining entirely — isolating the one feature that genuinely needs tight tolerance into a small machined insert, bolted or riveted into a sheet metal shell, usually costs less than machining the whole part just to get that one feature right. One Hybrid Assembly Example Plenty of real products aren't a clean either/or. A sheet metal chassis provides the lightweight, cost-effective structural shell, while CNC-machined brackets or mounting plates handle the specific spots that need tight tolerances a formed part can't hold — bolted or riveted into the sheet metal structure. A common version of this: a sheet-metal chassis with a CNC-machined bearing bracket bolted into it. The chassis handles the overall shape, mounting points, and structural panel work — all things sheet metal does well and cheaply at volume. The bearing bracket needs a precisely bored, tightly toleranced hole to seat a bearing correctly, which sheet metal forming can't reliably hold. Rather than machining the entire chassis to get that one bore right, the bore lives on a small dedicated machined part, and the two interfaces — chassis mounting holes and bracket mounting holes — are designed to align during assembly. This hybrid approach is common enough in electronics and equipment housings that it's worth considering from the start of a design, rather than defaulting to one process and forcing every feature to fit it. It's also one of the more practical reasons to source both processes from the same shop — fewer handoffs, fewer tolerance mismatches between the two parts when they're meant to bolt together. Our enclosure design guide goes deeper into this specific decision for enclosure design — covering the same choice this article addresses, but focused on the practical challenges of enclosure geometry, internal component fit, and assembly. Aluminum 5052 forms well and is a workhorse for sheet metal enclosures, but it's a softer alloy that machines less cleanly at tight tolerances than harder grades. Aluminum 6061 is the opposite pattern: it machines cleanly and holds tolerance well on a CNC part, but its formability is more limited — tight bend radii in 6061 are more prone to cracking than in 5052. 304 and 201 stainless steel both fabricate well as sheet metal for enclosures and structural panels, but on the machining side stainless work-hardens as it's cut, which means slower feeds, more tool wear, and a costlier part than the same geometry in aluminum or steel. Cold rolled steel is a common, economical choice for sheet metal work and machines acceptably too, which is part of why it shows up so often in both processes for general-purpose brackets and housings. If a design is locked into a specific alloy for strength, corrosion resistance, or cost reasons, it's worth checking that alloy's behavior in the process you're leaning toward before finalizing — a great geometry choice can still get expensive if the material fights the process. See our guide to sheet metal material types for a fuller breakdown by alloy. Types of Holes and CNC Hole Machining Explained In CNC machining, few operations challenge process control and tool stability as much as blind hole machining. A blind hole is a hole that terminates at a defined internal depth rather than breaking through the opposite surface. Because the cavity is enclosed at the bottom, chip evacuation, thermal behavior, tool wear, and dimensional accuracy become far more difficult to manage compared to through-hole machining. These constraints make blind holes indispensable yet technically demanding features across precision mechanical parts, sealed housings, consumer products, and structural components. When projects require consistently accurate blind hole drilling, tapping, or fine-tolerance cavity machining, J LCCNC provides reliable depth control , specialized tool paths, and clean internal finishes, supporting both prototypes and full production. What Is a Blind Hole? (Quora) A blind hole is defined by its closed end. Unlike a through hole, which passes entirely through a workpiece, a blind hole stops before reaching the opposite side. The bottom shape varies depending on the tool used: conventional drills produce conical bottoms, whereas flat-bottom drills and end mills generate planar surfaces suitable for precision assemblies or tapping. The engineering purpose of blind holes extends well beyond simply preventing penetration. In structural parts, maintaining a continuous opposite surface preserves rigidity, prevents stress risers, and helps sustain load paths. In pressurized or sealed systems—pneumatic housings, pump bodies, battery enclosures—blind holes prevent leakage of fluids or gases. In aesthetic or ergonomic products, they allow components to be fastened internally without exposing screw holes on the exterior. Blind holes essentially balance internal functionality with external appearance, mechanical strength, and environmental protection. Blind Hole vs Through Hole Through holes are straightforward to machine because chips naturally exit, tools experience less thermal stress, and depth accuracy is less sensitive. Blind holes demand precise programming—typically down to fractions of a millimeter—because any error may result in breakthrough. Through holes favor higher cutting speeds and simpler setups, whereas blind holes influence manufacturing costs due to slower feeds, peck cycles, coolant optimization, and bottom-clearance requirements. This difference in machining complexity explains why blind hole features often drive DFM (Design for Manufacturability) considerations. Types of Holes in CNC Machining Hole geometry in CNC machining reflects functional intent. Through holes support fasteners, shafts, dowel pins, and alignment features, making them ideal for high-speed fabrication. Countersunk holes allow screws to sit flush with the surface, maintaining flatness in precision mechanical surfaces. Counterbores accommodate socket-cap screws and create controlled seating planes for load-bearing joints. Within this landscape, blind holes occupy a specialized category. They enable internal threads, hidden fastening points, or mounting cavities that must not disturb the profile or sealing plane of the component. In industrial machinery, blind holes allow assembly without compromising fluid channels or structural ribs. In consumer electronics, they maintain the clean, uninterrupted outer surfaces expected from modern design. The choice between blind and through holes ultimately depends on the balance between manufacturability and functional necessity. Blind Hole Machining Explained (Science Direct) Blind hole machining is more complex than ordinary drilling because the tool must operate inside a confined cavity with no path for chips to escape. As the flutes fill with chips, heat rises sharply and causes accelerated tool wear or material hardening, especially in stainless steel and titanium. This is why blind hole drilling strategies emphasize controlled chip load, coolant access, and stable tool geometry. Drilling Blind Holes Standard twist drills are used for most metals, but they form a conical bottom that may not meet design requirements. When engineers need a flat-bottomed blind hole—for example, to optimize the thread engagement length or to improve seating conditions—a flat-bottom drill or end mill is applied. Peck drilling cycles become essential in deeper holes, where periodic retraction clears chips and reduces heat. In high-precision applications, depth is repeatedly verified using machine probing or tool setters to ensure no risk of breakthrough. Depth Control and Tool Selection Depth accuracy is one of the defining challenges in blind hole machining. CNC tools rely on tool length offsets, spindle probing, or laser measurement systems to maintain consistency. Carbide drills offer superior rigidity for deeper holes, while coatings such as TiAlN or AlTiN stabilize cutting edges under heat. The selected tool often reflects not only the material but also the hole’s final function—threaded, reamed, or used as a locating feature. Material Behavior in Blind Hole Drilling Aluminum machines easily but forms long, continuous chips that can clog a blind cavity unless chip-breaking geometries are used. Stainless steel hardens quickly under heat and demands strict lubrication control. Titanium concentrates heat at the cutting edge, often requiring through-tool coolant systems. Engineering plastics behave differently—they may melt or smear if spindle speeds are excessive. The interaction between tool, material, and confined cavity defines the entire machining strategy for blind holes. Blind Hole Tapping (Blind Hole Tap) (Science Direct) Blind hole tapping is one of the most technically sensitive procedures in CNC machining. Unlike through-hole tapping, where excess chips simply exit the opposite side, blind hole tapping traps chips at the bottom. If unmanaged, these chips compact and cause tap breakage. Bottoming Taps for Blind Holes A blind hole tap—usually a bottoming tap—features very little chamfer, enabling threads to form almost to the bottom of the cavity. This is crucial when the full thread depth is needed for load-bearing joints, especially in aerospace or automotive parts. Plug taps and taper taps have longer chamfers and are not suitable for holes where thread engagement must begin close to the bottom. Best Practices for Tapping Blind Holes Effective blind hole tapping relies on rigid tapping cycles, stable lubrication, and precise pilot hole sizing. In difficult materials, spiral-flute taps help extract chips upward, preventing compaction at the bottom of the hole. Thread milling is often chosen when the material is prone to chip welding or when the design requires extremely tight tolerance control. The entire process must anticipate torque spikes, potential chip packing, and sensitivity to tool wear. Designing Blind Holes for CNC Manufacturing Blind hole design affects machinability more than most engineers initially assume. Hole depth must align with available drill and tap geometries, ensuring that tools do not deflect excessively. The bottom clearance should reflect the type of threading operation planned, and thin walls around the hole must be avoided to prevent distortion during machining. Depth, Diameter, and Tolerance The ratio between hole depth and diameter heavily influences tool stability. Excessively deep blind holes increase the likelihood of tool vibration, poor chip evacuation, and dimensional variation. Tolerance selection must reflect not only fit and function but also the realities of machining inside a confined space. Surface finish is another consideration: smoother walls reduce thread friction, improve fastener performance, and reduce wear during repeated assembly cycles. FAQ What is the purpose of a blind hole? To enable internal mounting, threading, or functional cavities without penetrating the opposite surface, preserving structure, sealing integrity, or aesthetics. Why is blind hole machining more complex than through holes? Restricted chip flow, higher heat concentration, and tighter depth accuracy requirements. How are blind holes tapped successfully? With bottoming taps, rigid cycles, proper lubrication, and chip evacuation strategies such as spiral flutes or thread milling. What is blind hole drilling? A controlled-depth drilling process designed to terminate precisely before breakthrough. Verify Now Blog > 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling by: Mila Sep 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor 0402 capacitor 0603 capacitor 0402 vs 0603 capacitor A common misconception is that a larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better filtering performance. However, in high-speed PCB designs such as FPGA, SoC, and DDR applications, 0402 capacitors with a typical value of 0.1 μF are commonly placed near BGA core power pins instead of larger 0603 capacitors. For the same nominal capacitance, the key difference in 0402 vs 0603 capacitor performance is not how much charge the capacitor stores, but its equivalent series inductance (ESL). At lower frequencies, the performance difference between package sizes is usually less significant. As the operating frequency enters the MHz range and above, ESL increasingly affects the impedance and effective frequency range of a decoupling capacitor. The Underlying Principle: Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL) A surface-mount capacitor is not an ideal capacitor. Its equivalent circuit typically consists of an ideal capacitance (C), equivalent series resistance (ESR), and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL comes from the entire current path, including the internal electrodes, terminations, PCB pads, traces, and power/ground vias. Inductance opposes rapidly changing current, and its effect becomes more significant as frequency increases. Every capacitor has a self-resonant frequency (SRF): Operating frequency < SRF: The device behaves mainly as a capacitor and can perform its decoupling function normally. Operating frequency > SRF: The device gradually becomes inductive, and its high-frequency decoupling capability decreases. A higher self-resonant frequency generally means that a decoupling capacitor can maintain low impedance over a wider high-frequency range. For example, consider 0402 and 0603 capacitors with the same nominal capacitance of 0.1 μF: 0603 capacitor: Its larger body size generally results in a longer internal current path and higher intrinsic parasitic inductance. 0402 capacitor: Its smaller body size generally provides a shorter current path and lower intrinsic parasitic inductance. Therefore, under similar capacitance and component structures, a 0402 capacitor typically has lower parasitic inductance and a higher self-resonant frequency than a 0603 capacitor, making it more suitable for high-frequency decoupling. The actual ESL and SRF values should be verified from the component datasheet or the manufacturer's high-frequency model. PCB Pads and Vias Also Add Parasitic Inductance Engineers often focus only on the capacitor's intrinsic ESL specified in the datasheet. However, in a complete power delivery network, PCB pads, traces, and vias also introduce parasitic inductance and can sometimes have an even greater impact than the capacitor itself. In an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor comparison, the larger pads and spacing of a 0603 package can make the connection between the capacitor and power/ground vias longer. This additional trace length increases the total loop inductance. The smaller pads of a 0402 capacitor make it easier to place power and ground vias close to the component. When the PCB manufacturing and assembly processes allow it, microvias or Via-in-Pad can also be used to further shorten the current path and reduce the power-to-ground loop area. When an IC core suddenly draws high-frequency transient current, the total inductance of the current loop affects the power response. Even a capacitor with excellent electrical characteristics may provide limited high-frequency decoupling if the current path is too long. This is why the key advantage of a 0402 capacitor is not simply its smaller package size, but its ability to help create a smaller and lower-inductance current loop. （Optimized Layout） 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor: Advantages and Limitations Advantages of 0402 Capacitors Lower intrinsic parasitic inductance and typically higher SRF, providing better performance for high-frequency decoupling; Smaller pads allow the capacitor to be placed closer to BGA power pins and return paths, reducing the power-to-ground loop area; Higher placement density allows more decoupling capacitors to be placed around BGA devices, helping optimize PDN impedance; The smaller package makes it easier to implement compact power and ground via arrangements and, when supported by the PCB process, microvia or Via-in-Pad structures. Limitations of 0402 Capacitors In the same component series, the available capacitance and voltage-rating options may be more limited, while the actual effective capacitance can also decrease under DC bias; For the same capacitance and voltage rating, the component cost may be higher than that of a 0603 capacitor; Manual soldering is more difficult, with a higher risk of insufficient soldering or component loss, and mass production requires tighter stencil and placement process control; At relatively low frequencies, the performance difference between 0402 and 0603 is usually small, so a 0402 capacitor does not need to be selected simply because it is smaller. When to Use 0603 Capacitors They can generally provide sufficient performance in lower-frequency filtering applications; The larger package can make it easier to obtain suitable capacitance, voltage ratings, and mechanical reliability; They are easier to solder manually and can be suitable for general power filtering and decoupling applications where high-frequency performance is not the primary concern. Therefore, the choice between an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor should not be based on a fixed frequency boundary. As frequency increases, the ESL differences introduced by the component package and PCB mounting structure become increasingly important. The actual selection should consider effective capacitance, ESR, ESL, SRF, and the PCB layout together. Key Considerations for Decoupling Capacitor Selection and Layout Place decoupling capacitors as close as possible to BGA core power pins and other power pins that require high-frequency transient current. A 0402 capacitor is often preferred for these applications. The goal is to reduce the total parasitic inductance of the current loop and improve high-frequency PDN impedance. For DC-DC outputs and other applications where mounting inductance is less critical, 0603 or even 0805 packages can be selected according to effective capacitance, voltage rating, cost, and manufacturing requirements. Loop area is more important than package size alone. This is a common misconception in PCB decoupling. A 0402 capacitor placed far away from the IC power and return path may provide poorer high-frequency performance than a 0603 capacitor placed directly along the current path. Package size is only one factor affecting parasitic inductance. The total power-to-ground loop inductance is more important. Component placement, pad design, and via location all play an important role in PCB decoupling. Do not blindly move to a 0201 package. As the package becomes smaller, the reduction in ESL can provide diminishing returns because the PCB mounting structure can become a larger part of the total inductance. At the same time, soldering difficulty, placement requirements, and component costs may increase. A 0402 capacitor is therefore a common balance between performance, board space, and manufacturing cost in many high-speed PDN designs, although the final package should always be selected according to the specific device and manufacturing process. Common Misconceptions About Decoupling Capacitors ❌ Misconception 1: A larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better decoupling. ✅ Reality: Under the same effective capacitance and operating conditions, package size itself does not determine how much energy a capacitor stores. The high-frequency performance difference between an 0402 capacitor and a 0603 capacitor mainly comes from parasitic parameters associated with the capacitor and its PCB mounting structure, with ESL being an important factor. ❌ Misconception 2: If the capacitance is the same, the package does not matter. ✅ Reality: Even with the same nominal capacitance, different packages can have different ESL, ESR, and SRF characteristics. During decoupling capacitor selection and PDN impedance simulation, models that match the actual component and PCB mounting structure should be used whenever possible. Otherwise, the simulated impedance curve and resonance characteristics may differ significantly from the actual result. For high-speed PCB decoupling, component selection should therefore go beyond nominal capacitance. The package, effective capacitance, ESL, SRF, and—most importantly—the complete current-loop PCB layout should all be considered. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Can AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly in ADC PCB Design? by: Mila Sep 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout agnd vs dgnd mixed-signal PCB design ADC PCB layout When designing an ADC or DAC, one of the most common questions in PCB layout is how to handle the AGND and DGND pins. If a device has separate analog and digital ground pins, should they be connected directly, separated into different ground planes, or joined at a single point? This question is especially important in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design, where fast digital switching currents can potentially interfere with sensitive analog circuits. To understand the right approach to AGND vs DGND, the key is not simply whether the two grounds are connected, but how the return currents flow through the PCB. (schematic with AGND & GND) Why Do ADCs and DACs Have Separate AGND and DGND Pins? An ADC can be roughly understood as having two different domains. One side contains the sampling circuit, op amp, reference, comparator, PGA, DAC core, and analog bias circuits. These belong to the analog domain. The other side contains the SPI/I²C interface, digital logic, registers, clock, state machine, and other digital circuits. These belong to the digital domain. One of the biggest characteristics of digital circuits is that their current can change very quickly. For example, when an SPI interface operates at tens of MHz, every clock transition can generate transient current. These currents need to form a complete return path through the power and ground network. This is where the problem begins. Assume the digital return current is: ID = 50 mA and it flows through a PCB trace with only: R = 20 mΩ The resulting ground voltage variation is: V = IR = 50 mA × 20 mΩ = 1 mV. 1 mV may look very small, but it is not necessarily negligible for a high-resolution ADC. For example, consider a 16-bit ADC with a 2.5 V full-scale range: 1 LSB ≈ 2.5 V / 65536 ≈ 38.1 μV Therefore, a 1 mV ground voltage variation corresponds to approximately: 1 mV / 38.1 μV ≈ 26 LSB Of course, the actual ADC conversion error depends on how this ground disturbance couples into the analog input, reference, and internal circuits. However, this example illustrates an important point: For a high-precision ADC, the key concern is not simply how low the ground resistance is, but where the digital return current flows. This is one of the fundamental considerations in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly? In many designs, AGND and DGND ultimately connect to the same ground reference. However, there is an important condition: this does not mean that AGND and DGND can simply be connected with two arbitrary traces and left at that. If the ADC or DAC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND should be connected close to the device, follow the manufacturer's recommended layout. For many high-precision ADCs and DACs, the recommended PCB layout is designed to maintain a low-impedance, low-inductance connection between AGND and DGND while preventing digital return currents from flowing through sensitive analog areas. Therefore, AGND and DGND do not necessarily need to be electrically isolated. What matters more is controlling the return-current path. (return-current path) Why Ground Plane Splitting Can Cause More Problems In traditional PCB layout, it is common to see analog and digital areas separated into AGND and DGND regions, with the two planes connected at a single point. It may look like a professional solution, but there is an important question: What happens to the return current when a digital signal crosses from the digital area into the analog area? For high-speed digital signals, return current tends to follow the lowest-impedance path in the reference plane and is concentrated near the area directly underneath the signal trace. If the ground plane is split, the return current can no longer follow a short path underneath the signal. Instead, it may have to travel around the split. As the return path becomes longer, the loop area increases and parasitic inductance can also increase. This may result in more EMI and crosstalk rather than less. Therefore, splitting the ground plane does not automatically reduce noise. In some cases, it can actually make signal integrity and EMI problems worse. This is especially important when a high-speed signal crosses a ground-plane split. The return current is forced to take a longer path, which can increase the loop area and introduce additional noise. For this reason, a good mixed-signal PCB design does not simply focus on physically separating analog and digital grounds. It focuses on keeping the return-current paths controlled and predictable. Instead, different types of return current should follow appropriate paths and avoid sensitive circuits whenever possible. 1. Analog Input Return The reference ground for the analog input should be located as close as practical to the ADC's AGND. Avoid allowing the analog input return current to travel through the MCU area or other high-noise digital regions. 2. ADC Power Return The return path from the AVDD decoupling capacitor should be kept short and should return to the analog ground near the ADC. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor depends not only on whether the capacitor is present, but also on the loop formed by the power pin, capacitor, and ground connection. Keeping this loop small is an important part of good ADC PCB layout . 3. Digital Interface Return High-speed transitions on SPI signals such as SCLK, MOSI, MISO, and CS can generate high-frequency transient currents. These return currents should form a compact loop near the digital interface whenever possible, rather than flowing through sensitive analog ground regions. 4. AGND/DGND Connection Inside the PCB Layout Regardless of how the PCB is partitioned, AGND and DGND ultimately need to return to the same system reference ground. Whether the connection should use a single-point connection, a local connection, or a continuous ground plane depends on the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. So, what you really want to achieve is: Keep different types of return current on controlled paths rather than simply separating the two ground planes. Should You Use a Ferrite Bead Between AGND and DGND? This is one area where I would strongly recommend against blindly applying a common rule. A design like this is sometimes seen: AGND ─── Ferrite Bead ─── DGND The idea is that the ferrite bead can block digital noise from reaching the analog ground. In certain power-filtering applications, ferrite beads can indeed provide frequency-dependent impedance and help suppress high-frequency noise. However, ground is not simply a noise path. It is an important system reference and also provides return-current paths for signals. Once a frequency-dependent component is inserted between AGND and DGND, a voltage difference between the two ground domains can develop depending on the current and frequency. For high-precision ADCs and DACs, this ground potential difference can itself become a source of error or noise. Therefore, unless the device manufacturer specifically recommends it, do not add a ferrite bead between AGND and DGND simply because you have heard that analog and digital grounds should be isolated. When designing the board, pay particular attention to: Whether digital return current flows through sensitive analog areas Whether the analog input return path is short and well controlled Whether the ADC power-decoupling loop is compact Whether high-speed digital signals cross a ground-plane split Whether unnecessary impedance exists between AGND and DGND So, instead of simply thinking: "Analog ground must always be separated from digital ground." A more accurate way to think about AGND vs DGND is: The grounds can be shared, but the return currents should be controlled. The ground plane can remain continuous, but the paths taken by noise currents must be carefully managed. For ADCs, DACs, and other mixed-signal devices, good mixed-signal PCB design is not simply about physically isolating analog and digital ground. It is about using proper PCB layout, routing, decoupling, and return-path control to prevent digital noise from coupling into sensitive analog circuits. PCB Conformal Coating: Which Components Need Masking? by: Mila Sep 23,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB conformal coating Applying a conformal coating to the PCB during PCB assembly process can enhance the PCB's resistance to moisture, salt spray, dust, and corrosive environments. However, it is essentially an insulating protective film. For this reason, not every area of a PCB is suitable for direct coating. Areas that require electrical contact, mechanical movement, heat dissipation, or optical transmission can actually develop new reliability issues if they are improperly coated. Especially for the following components, applying conformal coating directly without proper masking can lead to a situation where the PCB has been coated for protection, but the product develops problems because critical areas were coated when they should not have been. So, let’s take a closer look at where PCB conformal coating needs special attention. 1. Connectors: Protect Electrical Contact Areas Connectors are usually one of the most important components to keep clear of conformal coating. The reason is simple: their contacts need to maintain reliable electrical contact. For example, if a connector contact normally has a contact resistance of only a few tens of mΩ, allowing conformal coating to enter the contact area essentially adds an insulating film between the mating surfaces. The problem can be even more complicated because some connectors may still work after the first few mating cycles, as the coating can be scraped away from the contact area. But that does not mean the connection will remain reliable. Over time, vibration, temperature and humidity cycling, coating residue, contamination, and oxidation of the contact surface can all increase contact resistance or cause intermittent contact. In actual PCB conformal coating applications, the electrical contact area, mating area, and other surfaces that must maintain reliable contact generally need to be masked. The exact masking area should be determined according to the connector manufacturer's coating requirements. This is especially important in automotive electronics and industrial control equipment that operate under long-term vibration. Being able to conduct electricity once does not necessarily mean the connection will remain reliable. （Connectors component） 2. Relays and Switches: Keep Contacts and Moving Parts Clear Contacts and moving mechanisms also require special attention, making relays another type of component that needs careful consideration during conformal coating. A relay typically contains contacts, an armature, springs, and other mechanical structures. If conformal coating enters the moving mechanism, it may affect the mechanical action of the relay. More importantly, the contacts themselves are critical because a relay relies on mechanical contacts to make and break an electrical circuit. If the contact surfaces are contaminated by coating, contact resistance, arcing characteristics, and long-term reliability may all be affected. Therefore, it does not mean that the entire relay must always be left uncoated. For sealed relays that have been verified as compatible with conformal coating, the outside of the component and the surrounding PCB may still be coated for protection. The areas that require particular attention are the contacts, moving mechanisms, and any areas specifically designated as coating-prohibited by the manufacturer. For high-voltage relays, additional considerations include creepage distance, clearance, and the effect of the coating on insulation performance. It should not simply be assumed that conformal coating automatically provides sufficient electrical isolation. 3. Buttons and Potentiometers: Avoid Coating Moving Contacts Components that contain moving or contacting mechanisms also require special attention. Mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components can be affected if conformal coating enters their internal moving or contact areas. For example, a potentiometer contains sliding contacts. If conformal coating penetrates into the mechanism, it can form a thin insulating contamination layer over the sliding contacts. What can happen? Resistance jumps, poor contact, and increased noise are all possible. This can be particularly troublesome in analog circuits because the problem may not appear as an obvious component failure. Instead, it may show up as increased output noise, ADC reading drift, or other intermittent problems that are difficult to trace. Therefore, for mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components, the masking area should be determined based on the component structure and manufacturer's requirements rather than simply applying full-component coating. （Buttons component） 4. Power Components: Consider Thermal Performance MOSFETs, DC-DC converters, LDOs, and other power components often have large copper areas around them to help dissipate heat. The effect of conformal coating on thermal performance cannot simply be described as "coating always causes the temperature to increase by a certain amount." Instead, the entire thermal path needs to be considered. For power components that rely on PCB copper, thermal vias, thermal pads, or external heat sinks for heat dissipation, the coating location, coating thickness, and overall mechanical design may all affect the final thermal performance. For example, assume a power component dissipates 2 W and its junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is 30 °C/W. Under this simplified model, the temperature rise is approximately: ΔT = P × θJA = 2 × 30 = 60 °C If the overall thermal conditions cause the effective thermal resistance to increase to 40 °C/W: ΔT = 2 × 40 = 80 °C Under this assumption, the temperature rise increases by 20 °C. It is important to note that this is only a simplified example showing how changes in thermal resistance affect temperature rise. It does not mean that conformal coating itself will necessarily increase θJA from 30 °C/W to 40 °C/W. The actual result depends on factors such as PCB copper area, thermal vias, component package, airflow, heat sink design, coating material, and coating thickness. Therefore, for high-power MOSFETs, power inductors, rectifier diodes, DC-DC converters, and similar components, the key question is whether the overall thermal path becomes less effective after coating. For thermal pads, thermal vias, exposed heat-dissipation surfaces, and areas that contact a heat sink, the need for masking should be determined based on the component and mechanical design rather than coating everything simply to achieve complete coverage. 5. Optical Components: Protect Optical Paths Conformal coating can also directly affect the performance of optical components. LEDs, photoelectric sensors, infrared receivers, cameras, light-sensitive devices, and similar components require particular attention. Conformal coating can change the transmittance, reflectivity, or surface condition of an optical window. For example, if a photoelectric sensor is calibrated for a specific optical window and an additional coating layer is applied to that surface, the optical path may change. As a result, sensors in the same production batch may produce inconsistent outputs. For components involving an optical path, first confirm with the component manufacturer whether conformal coating is permitted and what materials, coating thicknesses, and coverage areas are allowed. Do not assume that a coating will have no optical impact simply because the coating itself is transparent. 6. PCB Conformal Coating Is Not About Complete Coverage One of the most common mistakes in PCB conformal coating is treating complete coverage as the ultimate goal. A better approach is simple: protect the areas that need protection, and keep critical areas free of coating. During the PCB design stage, the coating requirements for different areas should be defined in advance. In general, they can be considered in three categories: Areas That Should Be Coated Exposed copper Solder joints General passive components and their soldered areas Areas that are vulnerable to moisture, salt spray, and corrosion Areas That Should Be Kept Free of Coating or Masked Electrical contact areas of connectors Moving or contacting mechanisms in buttons and potentiometers Test points Optical windows Other areas that need to maintain electrical or mechanical contact Components That Require Specification-Based Evaluation Power components Relays Transformers Sensors Crystals and oscillators Other specialized components The third category should not simply be classified as "coat" or "do not coat." The decision should be based on the component manufacturer's datasheet, coating compatibility, and the actual application environment. 7. How to Define Conformal Coating Areas During PCB Design Conformal coating should not be considered only after the PCB has been manufactured. The design stage should clearly define which areas require coating, which areas require masking, and what coating requirements need to be met. Coating Area Areas that require protection from moisture, contamination, corrosion, or other environmental factors. Keep-Out Area Areas that must remain free of conformal coating, such as connector contacts, test points, and optical windows. Masking Area Areas that need to be protected during manufacturing using masking tape, fixtures, or other masking methods. Thickness Requirement The target thickness of the conformal coating should be specified according to the application and material requirements. Inspection Requirement Quality requirements should be defined for coating coverage, missed coating, runs, bubbles, and other appearance or process-related defects. If you are sending your design for PCB production , it is recommended to clearly indicate the required coating and masking areas in the Gerber files, assembly drawings, or other production documentation. Conclusion Finally, do not rely only on the conformal coating manufacturer's documentation. The coating requirements of individual component manufacturers also need to be considered. For example, some connectors may allow coating while others explicitly prohibit it. Likewise, some MOSFETs may tolerate full coating, while others have thermal structures that require special treatment. Good PCB conformal coating design is not simply about maximizing coverage or increasing coating thickness. It is about clearly defining where coating should be applied, where it should not be applied, and why. The purpose of conformal coating is to improve PCB reliability in harsh environments, not to make the entire board look completely covered. By defining the Coating Area, Keep-Out Area, and Masking Area during the PCB design stage, the coating process and subsequent quality control can be much clearer and more reliable. PCB Conformal Coating: Which Components Need Masking? by: Mila Sep 23,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB conformal coating Applying a conformal coating to the PCB during PCB assembly process can enhance the PCB's resistance to moisture, salt spray, dust, and corrosive environments. However, it is essentially an insulating protective film. For this reason, not every area of a PCB is suitable for direct coating. Areas that require electrical contact, mechanical movement, heat dissipation, or optical transmission can actually develop new reliability issues if they are improperly coated. Especially for the following components, applying conformal coating directly without proper masking can lead to a situation where the PCB has been coated for protection, but the product develops problems because critical areas were coated when they should not have been. So, let’s take a closer look at where PCB conformal coating needs special attention. 1. Connectors: Protect Electrical Contact Areas Connectors are usually one of the most important components to keep clear of conformal coating. The reason is simple: their contacts need to maintain reliable electrical contact. For example, if a connector contact normally has a contact resistance of only a few tens of mΩ, allowing conformal coating to enter the contact area essentially adds an insulating film between the mating surfaces. The problem can be even more complicated because some connectors may still work after the first few mating cycles, as the coating can be scraped away from the contact area. But that does not mean the connection will remain reliable. Over time, vibration, temperature and humidity cycling, coating residue, contamination, and oxidation of the contact surface can all increase contact resistance or cause intermittent contact. In actual PCB conformal coating applications, the electrical contact area, mating area, and other surfaces that must maintain reliable contact generally need to be masked. The exact masking area should be determined according to the connector manufacturer's coating requirements. This is especially important in automotive electronics and industrial control equipment that operate under long-term vibration. Being able to conduct electricity once does not necessarily mean the connection will remain reliable. （Connectors component） 2. Relays and Switches: Keep Contacts and Moving Parts Clear Contacts and moving mechanisms also require special attention, making relays another type of component that needs careful consideration during conformal coating. A relay typically contains contacts, an armature, springs, and other mechanical structures. If conformal coating enters the moving mechanism, it may affect the mechanical action of the relay. More importantly, the contacts themselves are critical because a relay relies on mechanical contacts to make and break an electrical circuit. If the contact surfaces are contaminated by coating, contact resistance, arcing characteristics, and long-term reliability may all be affected. Therefore, it does not mean that the entire relay must always be left uncoated. For sealed relays that have been verified as compatible with conformal coating, the outside of the component and the surrounding PCB may still be coated for protection. The areas that require particular attention are the contacts, moving mechanisms, and any areas specifically designated as coating-prohibited by the manufacturer. For high-voltage relays, additional considerations include creepage distance, clearance, and the effect of the coating on insulation performance. It should not simply be assumed that conformal coating automatically provides sufficient electrical isolation. 3. Buttons and Potentiometers: Avoid Coating Moving Contacts Components that contain moving or contacting mechanisms also require special attention. Mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components can be affected if conformal coating enters their internal moving or contact areas. For example, a potentiometer contains sliding contacts. If conformal coating penetrates into the mechanism, it can form a thin insulating contamination layer over the sliding contacts. What can happen? Resistance jumps, poor contact, and increased noise are all possible. This can be particularly troublesome in analog circuits because the problem may not appear as an obvious component failure. Instead, it may show up as increased output noise, ADC reading drift, or other intermittent problems that are difficult to trace. Therefore, for mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components, the masking area should be determined based on the component structure and manufacturer's requirements rather than simply applying full-component coating. （Buttons component） 4. Power Components: Consider Thermal Performance MOSFETs, DC-DC converters, LDOs, and other power components often have large copper areas around them to help dissipate heat. The effect of conformal coating on thermal performance cannot simply be described as "coating always causes the temperature to increase by a certain amount." Instead, the entire thermal path needs to be considered. For power components that rely on PCB copper, thermal vias, thermal pads, or external heat sinks for heat dissipation, the coating location, coating thickness, and overall mechanical design may all affect the final thermal performance. For example, assume a power component dissipates 2 W and its junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is 30 °C/W. Under this simplified model, the temperature rise is approximately: ΔT = P × θJA = 2 × 30 = 60 °C If the overall thermal conditions cause the effective thermal resistance to increase to 40 °C/W: ΔT = 2 × 40 = 80 °C Under this assumption, the temperature rise increases by 20 °C. It is important to note that this is only a simplified example showing how changes in thermal resistance affect temperature rise. It does not mean that conformal coating itself will necessarily increase θJA from 30 °C/W to 40 °C/W. The actual result depends on factors such as PCB copper area, thermal vias, component package, airflow, heat sink design, coating material, and coating thickness. Therefore, for high-power MOSFETs, power inductors, rectifier diodes, DC-DC converters, and similar components, the key question is whether the overall thermal path becomes less effective after coating. For thermal pads, thermal vias, exposed heat-dissipation surfaces, and areas that contact a heat sink, the need for masking should be determined based on the component and mechanical design rather than coating everything simply to achieve complete coverage. 5. Optical Components: Protect Optical Paths Conformal coating can also directly affect the performance of optical components. LEDs, photoelectric sensors, infrared receivers, cameras, light-sensitive devices, and similar components require particular attention. Conformal coating can change the transmittance, reflectivity, or surface condition of an optical window. For example, if a photoelectric sensor is calibrated for a specific optical window and an additional coating layer is applied to that surface, the optical path may change. As a result, sensors in the same production batch may produce inconsistent outputs. For components involving an optical path, first confirm with the component manufacturer whether conformal coating is permitted and what materials, coating thicknesses, and coverage areas are allowed. Do not assume that a coating will have no optical impact simply because the coating itself is transparent. 6. PCB Conformal Coating Is Not About Complete Coverage One of the most common mistakes in PCB conformal coating is treating complete coverage as the ultimate goal. A better approach is simple: protect the areas that need protection, and keep critical areas free of coating. During the PCB design stage, the coating requirements for different areas should be defined in advance. In general, they can be considered in three categories: Areas That Should Be Coated Exposed copper Solder joints General passive components and their soldered areas Areas that are vulnerable to moisture, salt spray, and corrosion Areas That Should Be Kept Free of Coating or Masked Electrical contact areas of connectors Moving or contacting mechanisms in buttons and potentiometers Test points Optical windows Other areas that need to maintain electrical or mechanical contact Components That Require Specification-Based Evaluation Power components Relays Transformers Sensors Crystals and oscillators Other specialized components The third category should not simply be classified as "coat" or "do not coat." The decision should be based on the component manufacturer's datasheet, coating compatibility, and the actual application environment. 7. How to Define Conformal Coating Areas During PCB Design Conformal coating should not be considered only after the PCB has been manufactured. The design stage should clearly define which areas require coating, which areas require masking, and what coating requirements need to be met. Coating Area Areas that require protection from moisture, contamination, corrosion, or other environmental factors. Keep-Out Area Areas that must remain free of conformal coating, such as connector contacts, test points, and optical windows. Masking Area Areas that need to be protected during manufacturing using masking tape, fixtures, or other masking methods. Thickness Requirement The target thickness of the conformal coating should be specified according to the application and material requirements. Inspection Requirement Quality requirements should be defined for coating coverage, missed coating, runs, bubbles, and other appearance or process-related defects. If you are sending your design for PCB production , it is recommended to clearly indicate the required coating and masking areas in the Gerber files, assembly drawings, or other production documentation. Conclusion Finally, do not rely only on the conformal coating manufacturer's documentation. The coating requirements of individual component manufacturers also need to be considered. For example, some connectors may allow coating while others explicitly prohibit it. Likewise, some MOSFETs may tolerate full coating, while others have thermal structures that require special treatment. Good PCB conformal coating design is not simply about maximizing coverage or increasing coating thickness. It is about clearly defining where coating should be applied, where it should not be applied, and why. The purpose of conformal coating is to improve PCB reliability in harsh environments, not to make the entire board look completely covered. By defining the Coating Area, Keep-Out Area, and Masking Area during the PCB design stage, the coating process and subsequent quality control can be much clearer and more reliable.
