Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. PCB Layout Examples: From high-speed and RF to HDI, BGA, and rigid-flex designs, we handle a wide range of complex PCB layout requirements. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement by: Mila Sep 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout interface driver PCB connector placement interface PCB design People who design PCBs for embedded, industrial control, and communication hardware have probably heard a common PCB layout rule: interface drivers should be placed as close as possible to board-edge connectors. This is a practical guideline rather than an absolute requirement. For CAN and RS485, a slightly longer path may not immediately cause problems, while for high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe, longer traces can increase impedance discontinuities, parasitic effects, and return-path issues. If the driver is placed deep inside the board with a long trace between it and the connector, problems such as excessive radiated emissions, ESD-related MCU resets, closed high-speed eye diagrams, or communication errors may occur. This is why PCB connector placement and interface driver placement should be considered together in an interface PCB design . （Driver far from connector vs Driver close to connector ） 1. Three Common Types of Interface Drivers Interface drivers handle signal conversion and driving between the main controller on the PCB and external cables. Different interfaces have different transmission speeds, electrical standards, and communication protocols. From a functional perspective, they can be divided into three main categories. Level Translators / Interface Transceivers These devices primarily perform level conversion and interface adaptation, allowing two electrically incompatible systems on the PCB and external side to communicate correctly. RS232 transceiver (MAX232): Uses an internal charge pump to generate the positive and negative voltages required by RS-232. It converts TTL/CMOS logic levels on the MCU side into RS-232 levels, while the receiver performs the reverse conversion. RS-232 is a single-ended interface referenced to signal ground, not a differential interface. RS485/RS422 transceiver (MAX485): Converts single-ended TTL signals into differential signals and provides the drive capability required for long-distance bus transmission. CAN transceiver (TJA1050): Handles level conversion between the MCU logic side and the CAN bus, and drives and receives bus signals according to the dominant and recessive states defined by CAN. A practical CAN interface normally also requires external protection devices such as TVS diodes. High-Speed Physical Layer / PHY PHY devices for USB, Ethernet, HDMI/DisplayPort, and other high-speed interfaces integrate physical-layer functions for signal transmission and reception, including functions such as equalization and swing control. From a PCB layout perspective, controlled impedance, continuous reference planes, and an appropriate routing topology are required to maintain signal integrity. Differential impedance, such as 90Ω or 100Ω, is primarily determined by trace width, trace spacing, dielectric thickness, dielectric constant, and the reference plane. These parameters are implemented through the PCB stackup and routing design rather than being determined by the PHY itself. Differential Interface Drivers / Receivers Differential drivers and receivers such as LVDS and CML devices are used for high-speed point-to-point transmission. They precisely control differential common-mode voltage and signal swing to reduce jitter and overshoot during high-speed transmission. 2. Why Should Interface Drivers Usually Be Placed Close to Board-Edge Connectors? The following four factors apply differently depending on the interface type and should be evaluated as part of the overall interface PCB design. Shorten the Boundary Trace and Reduce EMI and ESD Risks Long traces between a connector and its driver increase the distance over which high-speed signals travel across the PCB and may increase the effective loop area of high-frequency currents. When the reference plane is discontinuous or the return path is interrupted, these traces are more likely to generate common-mode currents and additional EMI radiation. External ESD, surges, and environmental interference may also couple into the board through these paths. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens this section of the trace and reduces the high-frequency loop area, helping to lower the risk of radiated emissions and internal interference coupling. This can also reduce the workload during EMC debugging. However, EMI risk is not determined by trace length alone. Return paths, reference planes, loop area, signal edge rate, common-mode current, connector structure, and cable coupling all play important roles in PCB layout. Reduce Parasitic Effects and Maintain High-Speed Signal Integrity PCB traces inherently have parasitic capacitance and inductance. For high-speed differential interfaces such as USB, PCIe, MIPI, and HDMI, longer traces can increase the accumulated parasitic effects and make it more difficult to maintain impedance continuity. This can lead to slower signal edges, overshoot, ringing, and reflections, resulting in eye closure and increased bit error rates. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens the signal path, reduces unnecessary parasitic effects, and simplifies the routing topology, making it easier to maintain a continuous controlled-impedance transmission path. This is particularly important in high-speed interface PCB design. Shorten the ESD Discharge Path and Improve Protection Effectiveness Serial ports, Ethernet ports, and HDMI connectors are common entry points for ESD and surge energy. The effectiveness of ESD protection depends on many factors, including the type and location of the TVS device, dynamic clamping voltage, discharge path, grounding structure, PCB stackup, MCU tolerance, and interface isolation. It is therefore not determined by trace length alone. Placing the driver and ESD protection devices close to the connector and connecting them to the ground plane with short, direct traces helps provide a low-impedance discharge path. This reduces the risk of high-voltage pulses coupling into the core circuitry. During ESD testing, a system may experience MCU resets, communication errors, or, in severe cases, component damage. These problems need to be addressed through the overall protection architecture rather than relying on connector placement alone. Maintain a Continuous Path Between the Transceiver and Connector For differential interfaces such as RS485 and CAN, the relatively small signal swing makes differential transmission an important part of their noise immunity. Rather than simply assuming that the signal will experience significant amplitude loss along a long PCB trace, it is more important to consider whether the path between the transceiver and connector is short, continuous, and supported by a clear return path. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. Practical PCB Layout Guidelines for Interface Circuit Guideline 1: Typical Placement Order — Connector → Protection → Filtering / Common-Mode Processing → Interface Transceiver → Controller From the board edge toward the center, a common arrangement is: Outer edge: Board-edge connector; Protection layer: TVS diodes, ceramic discharge devices, gas discharge tubes, and other ESD protection components; Filtering / common-mode layer: Common-mode chokes, ferrite beads, and filtering capacitors; Driver layer: MAX485, PHY, CAN transceivers, and other interface ICs; Core circuitry: MCU/FPGA and other main processing devices. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller. Verify Now Blog > Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS by: Mila Sep 14,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout ESD protection esd protection circuit Previous articles have covered key technologies related to chip ESD, including ESD diodes, power clamps, CDM mechanisms, and ESD testing procedures, with a focus on chip-level electrostatic discharge protection. However, a common problem in real-world engineering applications is that an IC may pass all standard ESD tests but still suffer damage or failure when used on an actual customer circuit board. Engineers often assume that the problem is insufficient chip-level ESD protection. However, this judgment has limitations. Not all electrical failures are caused by ESD. In many real-world applications, the underlying cause may instead be EOS (Electrical Overstress). 1. What Is EOS? EOS stands for Electrical Overstress. It refers to a condition in which an IC is subjected to voltage, current, or power stress beyond its designed safe operating limits, resulting in electrical abnormalities or physical damage. Common EOS Scenarios EOS can occur in many real-world application conditions, including: Power supply overvoltage I/O input voltage exceeding the specified limit Output short circuits Hot-plugging transients Line surge events Power supply reversal Negative voltage stress Ground bounce Abnormal power sequencing EOS is not a single standardized failure test model. Instead, it is a general term for failures caused by excessive electrical stress. Any voltage, current, or power stress that exceeds the device's designed tolerance can potentially result in EOS failure. 2. Key Differences Between EOS and ESD Both ESD and EOS can cause electrical damage to an IC, which is why they are easily confused in engineering practice. However, they differ significantly in terms of stress characteristics, duration, energy, and failure mechanisms. （Comparison of ESD and EOS Waveforms） 3. Why Can an IC Fail After Passing ESD Tests? Passing standardized HBM and CDM tests only demonstrates that an IC can withstand specific short-duration electrostatic discharge stresses under defined test conditions. It does not mean that the device can withstand every type of electrical transient that may occur in a real system. Standard ESD Tests Have Limited Coverage Standard ESD tests are designed around defined test models and conditions. They verify whether an IC's ESD protection structures and discharge paths can safely handle specified electrostatic pulses. However, these tests cannot reproduce every electrical stress that may occur after the IC is integrated into a complete circuit board. Real-World Applications Introduce Different Electrical Stress In actual circuit board applications, electrical stress may come from: Cable insertion and removal Power-on overshoot External load short circuits Surge coupling through long cables Back-EMF from motors, relays, and other inductive loads Transient ground potential rise Abnormal sequencing between multiple power domains Accidental power connection Compared with standardized ESD pulses, these events may have longer durations, higher accumulated energy, or repeated stress characteristics, resulting in different types of IC damage. The internal ESD protection circuit of an IC is primarily designed to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses. Its purpose is to establish a controlled discharge path and divert transient energy. Therefore, passing ESD tests does not mean that an IC has system-level protection against all EOS conditions. （ESD Test PASS vs Real PCB FAIL） 4. The Functional Limits of Internal ESD Protection A common misconception in system design is that an IC can withstand all external electrical disturbances simply because its pins include an ESD protection circuit. In practice, this assumption can create significant reliability risks. What Is Internal ESD Protection Designed For? The internal ESD protection structure is an important protection layer against electrostatic events. It is designed to provide a low-impedance path for short-duration ESD currents and prevent excessive voltage from reaching sensitive internal circuits. However, this protection is not intended to absorb large amounts of energy for an extended period. It should therefore not be treated as a substitute for system-level EOS protection. What Happens Under Sustained Overvoltage? For example, if an I/O pin is continuously exposed to a voltage beyond its specified operating range and the internal protection structure enters conduction, current may continue to flow into or through the IC. As the stress continues, the protection device and related circuits can generate significant heat. Depending on the electrical stress and internal current path, this may eventually cause damage to components such as: I/O protection devices Output driver circuits Power clamp structures Metal interconnects Vias PN junctions Core input circuits The actual damage location depends on the magnitude and duration of the external stress as well as the current path inside the IC. Why Board-Level Protection Is Required A key engineering principle is that internal ESD protection is primarily intended to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses, while system-level electrical stress with significant energy should be limited and protected at the board level. Common board-level protection methods include: TVS devices Series current-limiting resistors Power clamps Fuses Overcurrent protection Appropriate grounding Proper PCB layout The goal is not simply to add more protection components, but to limit the voltage, current, and energy that can reach the IC and provide a controlled path for transient energy. （Board-Level Protection + IC Internal ESD Protection） 5. Typical EOS Damage Locations and Failure Analysis EOS damage is closely related to the actual current path created by the electrical stress. Different types of stress can affect different areas of the IC: Power supply overvoltage: May damage power clamp structures, internal power circuits, metal interconnects, and thin gate-oxide devices. I/O input overvoltage: May damage I/O protection structures, input circuits, pull-up or pull-down protection structures, and core gate circuits. Output short circuit: May damage output driver circuits, metal interconnects, vias, and local diffusion regions. Negative voltage stress: May damage I/O protection structures, junction regions, and input/output circuits. Therefore, EOS failure analysis should not rely solely on the appearance of a localized burn mark. It is more important to trace the source of the electrical stress, current entry and exit paths, stress duration, and energy to identify the root cause. 6. Engineering Differences Between ESD and EOS Failure Signatures There is no absolute method for distinguishing ESD from EOS based solely on physical failure signatures. However, practical failure analysis often reveals some characteristic differences that can be used as initial clues. Common ESD failure characteristics include: Localized single-point damage Gate-oxide breakdown Abnormalities around I/O protection structures Localized PN-junction leakage Leakage or parameter changes at a single pin Common EOS failure characteristics include: More obvious thermal damage Localized melting or burning of metal Significant thermal damage to vias or metal interconnects Large-area circuit damage Abnormalities along power paths Damage to output driver circuits Simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins or circuit nodes It is important to note that these failure signatures are only supporting evidence and should not be treated as final conclusions. Accurate differentiation between ESD and EOS failures requires comprehensive analysis of the failure scenario, electrical test data, application environment, test conditions, damage location, and physical analysis results. 7. The Risks of Misdiagnosing EOS as ESD In real-world applications, misdiagnosing an EOS failure as insufficient ESD protection can lead to an incorrect corrective strategy, wasting design resources while leaving the actual problem unresolved. When an IC is damaged by system-level EOS, simply increasing the size of the internal ESD protection structure, strengthening the internal power clamp, or widening internal metal interconnects generally cannot solve the system-level failure. The root cause may instead be related to board-level electrical stress, such as excessive external surge energy, improper TVS selection, continuous power supply overvoltage, load short circuits, abnormal hot-plug timing, or the lack of an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path for inductive loads. The key risk of misdiagnosing EOS is that engineers may continue to optimize the chip's ESD protection circuit without addressing the actual source and energy path of the system-level electrical stress. As a result, the same failure may occur repeatedly. Therefore, when investigating electrical failures in real-world applications, both chip-level and system-level factors should be considered rather than focusing only on the internal ESD structure. 8. Key Questions for Troubleshooting Suspected EOS Failures When an IC experiences an electrical failure, the following factors can be checked first to avoid automatically classifying the problem as an ESD failure: Failure Scenario Did the failure occur during a standard ESD test or during actual customer operation? Did it occur at the moment of power-up, during cable insertion or removal, after a load short circuit, or when a motor or relay was activated? Failure Location Is the problem limited to leakage at a single I/O pin, a low-resistance path between the power supply and ground, or simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins? Has the overall operating current of the IC changed significantly? Stress Characteristics Was the failure caused by a short-duration transient pulse, continuous overvoltage, or overcurrent? Was there any periodic or repeated electrical stress or abnormal power sequencing? Board-Level Protection Does the circuit board include TVS or other surge protection? Is an appropriate current-limiting circuit provided? Does the power supply have overvoltage or clamping protection? Does the grounding path provide sufficiently low impedance? Does the inductive load have an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path? These factors can help determine whether the failure is related to system-level EOS and provide a basis for tracing the electrical stress path into the IC. Conclusion Both ESD and EOS can cause IC leakage, short circuits, functional abnormalities, and physical damage, but their stress characteristics, protection strategies, and corrective measures are significantly different. Passing standard ESD tests only verifies the IC's ability to withstand specific short-duration electrostatic pulses and does not cover every overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, power reversal, or ground-bounce condition that may occur in a real system. Therefore, when investigating an IC failure in an actual application, engineers should not determine the root cause solely based on the fact that the device passed ESD testing or on the appearance of localized physical damage. Instead, the failure scenario, electrical stress, failure location, current path, board-level protection, and physical analysis results should be considered together. For electrical stress outside standard ESD test conditions, such as overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, and inductive load transients, EOS should be considered as a potential root cause. Appropriate board-level protection can help limit the voltage, current, and energy reaching the IC and reduce the risk of application-level failure. Why No Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator in PCB Layout? by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb routing crystal oscillator pcb layout pcb crystal oscillator When designing a PCB, many engineers have heard the rule: no traces should run under a crystal oscillator. But why? Can a low-speed signal trace really affect a crystal oscillator? And can a guard ring with grounding vias completely eliminate interference? Although a crystal oscillator provides the clock signal for digital circuits, its oscillation loop is highly sensitive to parasitic capacitance and external noise. Poor crystal oscillator PCB layout and PCB routing can cause frequency shifts, startup problems, or unstable clock signals, and may even increase EMI risks. So, why should traces be kept away from the area beneath a crystal? How should the guard ring and grounding vias be designed? Let's start with how a crystal oscillator works and then look at the key considerations for its PCB layout and routing. 1. How Does a Crystal Oscillator Work? A crystal oscillator uses the piezoelectric properties of a quartz crystal to generate a stable periodic signal. When an alternating voltage is applied to the crystal, it mechanically vibrates at a specific resonant frequency. The electrical and mechanical characteristics of the crystal allow it to provide a highly stable frequency reference for the circuit. In many digital systems, the crystal is connected to an oscillator circuit inside an MCU, processor, or other IC. A common configuration is the Pierce oscillator, where the crystal works together with two load capacitors to form the oscillation loop. The crystal itself can be considered as a high-Q resonant component. This means that even small changes in the surrounding circuit can affect its behavior. Therefore, crystal oscillator PCB layout is not simply about placing the component close to the IC. The routing, ground plane, surrounding copper, and parasitic effects also need to be considered. （Piezoelectric Effect） 2. Why Should You Avoid Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator? The area around a crystal oscillator may look electrically simple, but PCB routing underneath the crystal can introduce several unwanted effects. Parasitic Capacitance A PCB trace running underneath the crystal or its oscillator pins can form parasitic capacitance with the copper layers below or above it. This additional capacitance changes the effective load seen by the oscillator circuit. As a result, the crystal's oscillation frequency may shift, and the startup characteristics can also be affected. This is especially important because the crystal oscillator circuit usually operates with relatively small signal levels and is sensitive to its load conditions. Keeping unnecessary copper and traces away from the crystal area helps reduce these unpredictable parasitic effects. （recommend pcb layout） Noise Coupling High-speed signal traces can generate rapidly changing electric fields. If these traces pass beneath or too close to the crystal oscillator, noise can couple into the sensitive oscillation loop through parasitic capacitance. The problem becomes more noticeable when the nearby traces carry high-speed clocks, switching signals, or other signals with large voltage transitions. For this reason, good PCB routing practice is to keep noisy signal traces away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. EMI and Signal Integrity The crystal oscillator area should also be treated as a sensitive clock source. Poor routing can increase unwanted coupling between the oscillator and nearby circuits. At the same time, the crystal circuit itself can become a source of electromagnetic radiation if its return path and surrounding copper are not properly controlled. A compact layout with short connections and a clean reference plane can help reduce both noise coupling and EMI risks. （Sources of EMI Issues） 3. Why Use a Guard Ring and Grounding Vias? In addition to keeping signal traces away, some designs use a grounded copper guard ring around the crystal oscillator. Guard Ring A guard ring is a copper area surrounding the sensitive crystal circuit and connected to ground. Its purpose is to provide a low-impedance ground barrier around the oscillator area, helping reduce coupling from nearby signals. The guard ring should not replace the basic keep-out requirements. It is an additional measure for improving isolation and controlling the electromagnetic environment around the crystal. （Ground Guard Ring） Grounding Via Stitching Grounding vias can be placed around the guard ring to connect the surrounding ground copper to the ground planes on other layers. This via stitching helps maintain a more continuous ground structure and can reduce the path through which external noise couples into the oscillator area. However, adding more vias does not automatically make the design better. The via placement should be coordinated with the crystal package, oscillator pins, routing space, and PCB manufacturing requirements. （Ground Stitching Vias） Keep-Out Area The most basic rule is still to keep unnecessary signal traces and copper away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. The exact keep-out size depends on the crystal, IC, PCB stackup, operating frequency, and layout requirements. Therefore, the IC or crystal manufacturer's recommendations should be followed whenever available. A typical layout can be organized as: Crystal → Short oscillator traces → Load capacitors → IC. The surrounding area can then use a grounded guard ring and stitching vias where necessary. （typical crystal pcb layout） 4. Crystal Oscillator PCB Layout and Routing Tips Good crystal oscillator PCB layout focuses on keeping the oscillation loop short, quiet, and predictable. Place the Crystal Close to the IC The crystal should normally be placed as close as practical to the corresponding oscillator pins of the MCU or other IC. Shorter connections reduce parasitic capacitance and inductance and help minimize the area of the sensitive oscillator loop. Avoid placing the crystal far away and routing long traces back to the IC. Keep Oscillator Routing Short and Symmetrical The traces between the crystal and the oscillator pins should be as short as practical. Avoid unnecessary vias, sharp detours, and long parallel runs with noisy signals. When possible, keep the two oscillator connections reasonably symmetrical to reduce differences in parasitic effects. Place Load Capacitors Close to the Oscillator Pins Load capacitors are normally placed close to the crystal and IC oscillator pins. Long traces between the capacitors and the IC add parasitic inductance and capacitance, making the actual load different from the nominal capacitor value. Therefore, component placement and PCB routing should be considered together rather than separately. Avoid High-Speed Traces Near the Crystal During PCB routing, keep high-speed clocks, switching nodes, power converters, and other noisy signals away from the crystal area whenever possible. If a high-speed signal must cross the region, consider whether the routing can be changed to maintain sufficient physical separation. This is particularly important for dense multilayer boards where signals on adjacent layers may also couple through the dielectric. Provide a Clean Ground Reference A continuous ground plane can provide a stable reference for the surrounding circuit and help control return-current paths. However, avoid routing unrelated signals through the sensitive crystal area on other layers. The goal is not simply to create as much copper as possible, but to create a predictable electromagnetic environment around the oscillator. Consider the Crystal Package and Shielding For some applications, the crystal oscillator may be enclosed in a metal package or shielded structure. If shielding is used, make sure its connection to ground is reliable and that the mechanical structure does not introduce unexpected parasitic effects. For designs with strict clock stability or EMI requirements, testing should be used to verify the actual performance rather than relying only on layout rules. 5. Common Mistakes in Crystal Oscillator PCB Routing Several layout mistakes can make an otherwise functional crystal oscillator less stable. Running signal traces directly underneath the crystal. Routing high-speed or switching signals too close to the oscillator loop. Placing the crystal too far from the IC. Using unnecessarily long oscillator traces. Placing load capacitors far from the oscillator pins. Adding excessive vias or complicated routing around the crystal. Ignoring the IC manufacturer's crystal layout recommendations. These problems may not always cause an immediate failure. In some designs, the oscillator may still start normally but show frequency deviation, increased sensitivity to noise, or different behavior between PCB revisions. That is why crystal oscillator layout should be treated as a complete circuit rather than simply a component placement rule. The rule of “no traces under the crystal oscillator” is not an absolute manufacturing requirement. Its purpose is to reduce parasitic capacitance, noise coupling, and interference around a sensitive oscillator circuit. In practical PCB routing , the most important principles are to keep the crystal close to the IC, minimize the oscillator loop, keep noisy signals away, place load capacitors properly, and provide a clean ground environment. For more demanding designs, a grounded guard ring and via stitching can provide additional isolation. Ultimately, the recommended layout from the IC and crystal manufacturers should be used as the primary reference, with actual testing used to verify oscillator stability and EMI performance. But why? Can a low-speed signal trace really affect a crystal oscillator? And can a guard ring with grounding vias completely eliminate interference? Although a crystal oscillator provides the clock signal for digital circuits, its oscillation loop is highly sensitive to parasitic capacitance and external noise. As a result, the crystal's oscillation frequency may shift, and the startup characteristics can also be affected. This is especially important because the crystal oscillator circuit usually operates with relatively small signal levels and is sensitive to its load conditions. Keeping unnecessary copper and traces away from the crystal area helps reduce these unpredictable parasitic effects. （recommend pcb layout） Noise Coupling High-speed signal traces can generate rapidly changing electric fields. If these traces pass beneath or too close to the crystal oscillator, noise can couple into the sensitive oscillation loop through parasitic capacitance. The problem becomes more noticeable when the nearby traces carry high-speed clocks, switching signals, or other signals with large voltage transitions. For this reason, good PCB routing practice is to keep noisy signal traces away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. At the same time, the crystal circuit itself can become a source of electromagnetic radiation if its return path and surrounding copper are not properly controlled. A compact layout with short connections and a clean reference plane can help reduce both noise coupling and EMI risks. （Sources of EMI Issues） 3. Why Use a Guard Ring and Grounding Vias? Its purpose is to provide a low-impedance ground barrier around the oscillator area, helping reduce coupling from nearby signals. The guard ring should not replace the basic keep-out requirements. It is an additional measure for improving isolation and controlling the electromagnetic environment around the crystal. （Ground Guard Ring） Grounding Via Stitching Grounding vias can be placed around the guard ring to connect the surrounding ground copper to the ground planes on other layers. This via stitching helps maintain a more continuous ground structure and can reduce the path through which external noise couples into the oscillator area. However, adding more vias does not automatically make the design better. The via placement should be coordinated with the crystal package, oscillator pins, routing space, and PCB manufacturing requirements. （Ground Stitching Vias） Keep-Out Area The most basic rule is still to keep unnecessary signal traces and copper away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. The exact keep-out size depends on the crystal, IC, PCB stackup, operating frequency, and layout requirements. Therefore, the IC or crystal manufacturer's recommendations should be followed whenever available. A typical layout can be organized as: Crystal → Short oscillator traces → Load capacitors → IC. The surrounding area can then use a grounded guard ring and stitching vias where necessary. （typical crystal pcb layout） 4. Verify Now Blog > Sheet Metal Tapping Design Guidelines Sheet Metal Tapping Design Guidelines by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Tapping This guideline aims to provide structural engineers and mechanical designers with Design for Manufacturability (DFM) specifications for thread tapping in sheet metal fabrication and CNC milling/turning processes. It helps designers effectively avoid tool chipping, thread stripping, bend deformation, and engineering question (EQ) delays during the design phase—thereby significantly improving the automated DFM review approval rate, eliminating redundant back-and-forth communication, and substantially reducing order lead times and processing schedules. 1. Key Sheet Metal Tapping Parameters In sheet metal cutting and CNC machining, tapping is a critical process that creates internal threads in pre-machined pilot holes to allow direct fastening with bolts and screws. Compared to traditional methods like adding clinching nuts (PEM Nuts) or using clearance holes with standard nuts, direct tapping significantly reduces the bill of materials (BOM), lowers assembly labor, and achieves exceptional surface flatness. Thread Engagement: The percentage of overlapping profile depth between the external and internal threads. Thread engagement directly determines the pull-out strength of the threaded connection and the difficulty of machining. Thread Pitch: The axial distance between corresponding points on adjacent thread teeth. Metric threads express this as pitch in millimeters (e.g., M4 × 0.7), while Imperial threads express it as threads per inch (TPI, e.g., 1/4-20). Tap Drill Size (Pilot Hole Diameter): The pre-drilled or laser-cut hole diameter prior to tapping. An undersized hole can cause tap breakage or binding, whereas an oversized hole results in insufficient thread height and stripped threads. 2. Thread Engagement & Geometric Calculations When designing tapped parts, avoid blindly striving for 100% thread height. Research and engineering practice demonstrate that a thread engagement of 60% to 75% provides 100% of the bolt's ultimate tensile strength; further increasing engagement exponentially increases cutting torque and tap breakage risks. Thread Engagement Formula Thread Engagement (%) = [ (D_major - D_hole) / (1.08253 × P) ] × 100% (Note: Major Thread Diameter D_major and Pilot Hole Diameter D_hole are in mm; Pitch P is in mm) Recommended Thread Engagement by Material Soft Materials (Aluminum 6061-T6, Copper, Engineering Plastics POM/PA): A 70% to 75% thread engagement is recommended to achieve higher shear strength. Hard Materials (Stainless Steel 304/316, Carbon Steel, Titanium Alloys): A 50% to 60% thread engagement is recommended to significantly reduce tool wear and work-hardening risks. Sheet Thickness to Engagement Depth Ratio The optimal effective thread engagement length should reach 1.0 to 1.5 times the nominal bolt diameter (e.g., the effective depth for an M4 thread should be between 4 mm and 6 mm). For thin sheet metal where the plate thickness is less than 1.0 times the thread diameter, extruded/flanged hole tapping processes can be used to extend engagement depth. 3. Sheet Metal vs. CNC Machining Tapping Guidelines Laser-cut sheet metal and solid CNC machined parts differ fundamentally in tapping processes and must follow distinct geometric constraints: 4. Core Sheet Metal Tapping DFM Rules Clearance from Bends and Features When placing tapped holes near sheet metal bend lines, tensile stresses during bending cause thread distortion, preventing proper bolt insertion. Bend Clearance Rule: The distance from the tapped hole center to the bend line must be ≥ (1/2 × Bend Die Opening Width + 2 × Sheet Thickness). Feature Clearance Rule: Tapped hole edges must maintain a distance of at least 1.5 × Sheet Thickness from other cut features (e.g., large cutouts, slots). Tool Clearance and Fixture Interference Automated tapping machines and CNC tapping heads require adequate clearance. If a tapped hole is close to high vertical walls or internal cavity corners, the tapping chuck will collide. Geometric Interference Warning: Ensure a cylindrical clearance area above the tapped hole axis with a radius of at least 20 mm and no height obstructions to allow unhindered spindle entry. Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ) & Thermal Expansion Compensation Strategy: Laser cutting creates a micro-hardened layer (HAZ) along the hole wall. Verify Now Blog > Sheet Metal Tapping Design Guidelines Sheet Metal Tapping Design Guidelines by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in Tapping This guideline aims to provide structural engineers and mechanical designers with Design for Manufacturability (DFM) specifications for thread tapping in sheet metal fabrication and CNC milling/turning processes. It helps designers effectively avoid tool chipping, thread stripping, bend deformation, and engineering question (EQ) delays during the design phase—thereby significantly improving the automated DFM review approval rate, eliminating redundant back-and-forth communication, and substantially reducing order lead times and processing schedules. 1. Key Sheet Metal Tapping Parameters In sheet metal cutting and CNC machining, tapping is a critical process that creates internal threads in pre-machined pilot holes to allow direct fastening with bolts and screws. Compared to traditional methods like adding clinching nuts (PEM Nuts) or using clearance holes with standard nuts, direct tapping significantly reduces the bill of materials (BOM), lowers assembly labor, and achieves exceptional surface flatness. Thread Engagement: The percentage of overlapping profile depth between the external and internal threads. Thread engagement directly determines the pull-out strength of the threaded connection and the difficulty of machining. Thread Pitch: The axial distance between corresponding points on adjacent thread teeth. Metric threads express this as pitch in millimeters (e.g., M4 × 0.7), while Imperial threads express it as threads per inch (TPI, e.g., 1/4-20). Tap Drill Size (Pilot Hole Diameter): The pre-drilled or laser-cut hole diameter prior to tapping. An undersized hole can cause tap breakage or binding, whereas an oversized hole results in insufficient thread height and stripped threads. 2. Thread Engagement & Geometric Calculations When designing tapped parts, avoid blindly striving for 100% thread height. Research and engineering practice demonstrate that a thread engagement of 60% to 75% provides 100% of the bolt's ultimate tensile strength; further increasing engagement exponentially increases cutting torque and tap breakage risks. Thread Engagement Formula Thread Engagement (%) = [ (D_major - D_hole) / (1.08253 × P) ] × 100% (Note: Major Thread Diameter D_major and Pilot Hole Diameter D_hole are in mm; Pitch P is in mm) Recommended Thread Engagement by Material Soft Materials (Aluminum 6061-T6, Copper, Engineering Plastics POM/PA): A 70% to 75% thread engagement is recommended to achieve higher shear strength. Hard Materials (Stainless Steel 304/316, Carbon Steel, Titanium Alloys): A 50% to 60% thread engagement is recommended to significantly reduce tool wear and work-hardening risks. Sheet Thickness to Engagement Depth Ratio The optimal effective thread engagement length should reach 1.0 to 1.5 times the nominal bolt diameter (e.g., the effective depth for an M4 thread should be between 4 mm and 6 mm). For thin sheet metal where the plate thickness is less than 1.0 times the thread diameter, extruded/flanged hole tapping processes can be used to extend engagement depth. 3. Bend Clearance Rule: The distance from the tapped hole center to the bend line must be ≥ (1/2 × Bend Die Opening Width + 2 × Sheet Thickness). Feature Clearance Rule: Tapped hole edges must maintain a distance of at least 1.5 × Sheet Thickness from other cut features (e.g., large cutouts, slots). Tool Clearance and Fixture Interference Automated tapping machines and CNC tapping heads require adequate clearance. If a tapped hole is close to high vertical walls or internal cavity corners, the tapping chuck will collide. Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. events.before: Resources / 3D Printing Design / PETG 3D Printing Filament: Materials, Properties, and Uses PETG 3D Printing Filament: Materials, Properties, and Uses Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Dr. Mahder Tewolde PhD 19 min read Published September 19, 2022 Updated August 19, 2026 PETG 3D printing filament is a glycol-modified version of polyethylene terephthalate (PET), known for its strength, flexibility, and moderate chemical resistance. PETG offers good durability and moderate-to-high impact resistance among 3D printing filaments. The filament is used in various industries for applications (protective enclosures, mechanical components, prototypes, and outdoor parts) that need to withstand mild environmental conditions (exposure to moisture, but not extended UV exposure). Its ability to maintain structural integrity under mechanical stress and its ease of use make it an essential material in 3D printing. PETG filament is favored in high-volume 3D printing environments for its combination of strength, ductility, and printability, positioning it as a go-to choice for practical applications. The widespread use of PETG filament highlights its growing importance in hobbyist and industrial 3D printing sectors in functional part production. What is PETG Filament? PETG Filament is a thermoplastic 3D printing material defined as a Glycol-modified polyethylene terephthalate, which is not a copolyester but a modified homopolymer and recognized under the names PETG and PET-g filament. PETG Filament combines the chemical backbone of PET with glycol modification that reduces crystallinity, stabilizes melt behavior, and improves layer bonding, which supports adoption across consumer and industrial additive manufacturing workflows. A common functional printing material is polyethylene terephthalate glycol-modified (PETG) filament because it offers balanced toughness, moderate chemical resistance, and good dimensional stability without the high brittleness typical of highly crystalline polymers. PETG Filament demonstrates reliable printability through consistent extrusion flow and strong interlayer adhesion, with lower warping than Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) on common fused deposition modeling platforms. PETG Filament provides mechanical strength through high impact resistance, moderate tensile strength, and ductile failure behavior that suits enclosures, fixtures, and mechanical housings, with outdoor use dependent on UV exposure and environmental conditions. The Filament maintains structural performance under moderate repeated stress while supporting smooth surface finish and limited post-processing methods such as vapor smoothing, but supports sanding and machining, reinforcing material selection for functional end-use parts where thermal and fatigue limits remain controlled. "PETG stands out as a practical middle-ground material in 3D printing, balancing strength, ductility, and print reliability without the processing demands of higher-temperature polymers. Glycol modification reduces crystallinity, which supports strong layer adhesion, low warping, and consistent extrusion across both consumer and industrial workflows. Its mechanical toughness, moisture resistance, and moderate heat tolerance make it well suited for functional parts such as enclosures, fixtures, and outdoor components with limited UV exposure. As a result, PETG has become a dependable workhorse filament, reflecting the growing demand for materials that perform reliably under real-world mechanical and environmental conditions." Dr. Mahder Tewolde PhD What Type of Polymer is PETG? PETG is a glycol-modified polyethylene terephthalate classified as an amorphous thermoplastic polyester. PETG is synthesized by modifying the polymerization of PET with glycol (typically CHDM) to prevent crystallinity and enhance processing that disrupts crystallinity, reduces internal stress during cooling, and stabilize melt behavior during fused deposition modeling. Transparency, moderate chemical resistance, impact toughness, and ductility make PETG suitable for functional 3D printed parts that are required to withstand harsh environments and maintain dimensional consistency. PETG offers advantages for 3D printing through strong layer adhesion, relatively low shrinkage compared to ABS, and improved resistance to brittle fracture under mechanical load. PETG differs from Polylactic Acid (PLA) through higher impact resistance and improved thermal stability, while PLA emphasizes stiffness, dimensional accuracy, and ease of extrusion. ABS emphasizes higher heat resistance and rigidity, while PETG presents lower warping behavior and lower odor and particulate emissions during printing. PETG occupies a middle ground among common 3D printing polymers by balancing strength, toughness, and print reliability for applications including mechanical housings, protective enclosures, and outdoor components as a Polymer Material . What is PETG Filament Made Of? PETG is made by modifying polyethylene terephthalate (PET) with glycol, forming an amorphous thermoplastic polyester. with reduced crystallinity and improved melt stability. PETG Filament consists of long polymer chains built from terephthalic acid, ethylene glycol, and glycol modifiers that interrupt regular molecular packing and limit crystalline growth during cooling. The filament exhibits a predominantly amorphous polymer structure with limited crystallinity that supports consistent extrusion, strong interlayer bonding, and good dimensional stability during fused deposition modeling. PETG Filament demonstrates balanced 3D printing behavior through controlled melt flow, reduced internal stress during cooling, and improved resistance to brittle fracture under mechanical loading. Polylactic Acid relies on aliphatic polyester chains derived from lactic acid and emphasizes stiffness, surface quality, and low processing temperature. Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) relies on a rubber-toughened petroleum-based polymer structure that emphasizes heat resistance and rigidity while introducing higher shrinkage and warping tendencies. PETG Filament occupies a middle position between Polylactic Acid and Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene, combining toughness, moderate chemical resistance, and reliable print performance for functional parts under UV and temperature exposure. Is PETG Considered a Plastic? Yes, PETG is considered a thermoplastic polymer used in manufacturing and additive manufacturing. PETG belongs to the copolyester family and forms through copolymerization of polyethylene terephthalate with glycol modifiers, producing a melt-processable material with reduced crystallinity and stable melt behavior. PETG appears in 3D printing, packaging, and industrial applications because the material offers toughness, moderate chemical resistance, and dimensional stability under mechanical stress and controlled environmental exposure as a plastic material . What are the Properties of PETG Filament? The properties of PETG Filament are listed below. Melting Point : PETG Filament does not present a sharp melting point because glycol modification reduces crystallinity, producing a broad softening range that supports smooth extrusion during fused deposition modeling. Glass Transition Temperature : PETG Filament reaches glass transition in the range of 75 to 85 degrees Celsius, defining the temperature range where the material transitions from rigid behavior to rubber-like deformation under load. Temperature Resistance : PETG Filament maintains structural integrity at moderate service temperatures and resists deformation better than low-temperature polymers such as PLA under sustained heat exposure. Flexibility : PETG Filament demonstrates moderate flexibility through ductile deformation rather than brittle fracture, supporting impact resistance and load-bearing performance in functional parts. UV Resistance : PETG Filament offers moderate resistance to ultraviolet exposure, supporting limited outdoor use with gradual degradation unless UV stabilizers or protective coatings are applied. Hygroscopicity : PETG Filament absorbs moisture from the environment at a moderate rate, requiring dry storage conditions to preserve surface finish and extrusion consistency during printing. Heat Resistance : PETG Filament resists thermal softening better than PLA under continuous mechanical stress while remaining below the heat tolerance of high-temperature engineering plastics. What is the density of PETG? The density of PETG is approximately 1.27 grams per cubic centimeter or 1270 kilograms per cubic meter. PETG density reflects a relatively compact polymer structure that contributes to part weight and dimensional stability, while resistance to deformation depends primarily on mechanical properties rather than density alone. PETG density influences printed component mass, producing parts heavier than PLA, while improved impact resistance and structural reliability result from polymer toughness and ductile deformation in functional applications. What is the glass transition temperature of PETG? The glass transition temperature of PETG is 80 degrees Celsius. PETG reaches glass transition near that temperature range where the polymer transitions from rigid solid behavior to rubber-like deformation, representing an approximate upper limit for dimensional stability under sustained load. PETG glass transition temperature supports strong layer adhesion by allowing interlayer diffusion when deposited above glass transition, while shape retention during cooling results from gradual solidification as the material cools below that threshold. What is the heat resistance of PETG? The heat resistance of PETG under continuous mechanical load ranges up to 60 to 70 degrees Celsius before noticeable softening and creep occur, depending on part geometry and load conditions. PETG maintains limited structural stability below its glass transition temperature, supporting functional parts exposed to moderate heat, while deformation increases rapidly as temperatures approach glass transition. PETG shows higher heat resistance than Polylactic Acid at 55 to 60 degrees Celsius, while remaining below Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene, which tolerates continuous service temperatures near 80 to 85 degrees Celsius. Does PETG Shrink? Yes, PETG shrinks during cooling, although shrinkage remains low compared to thermoplastics used in fused deposition modeling. PETG shrinkage results from thermal contraction as extruded material transitions from melt to solid, introducing limited dimensional change and reduced warping risk. PETG maintains print stability through controlled cooling, consistent bed adhesion, moderate build plate temperatures, and reduced internal stress resulting from glycol modification. Is PETG Waterproof? Yes, PETG is considered waterproof in practical use because the polymer exhibits very low water absorption and does not dissolve or chemically degrade when exposed to moisture. PETG forms polymer chains with low permeability that limit water penetration, while strong interlayer adhesion during printing supports waterproof parts when extrusion parameters achieve adequate layer fusion. PETG suits applications involving liquid contact and limited outdoor exposure, while prolonged immersion or insufficient layer bonding introduces seepage risk through interlayer gaps rather than through the polymer material itself. Is PETG Hygroscopic? Yes, PETG is hygroscopic and absorbs moisture from the surrounding environment over time. PETG moisture absorption occurs at a lower rate than nylon and also lower than Polylactic Acid (PLA), explaining sensitivity to ambient humidity during storage. PETG moisture content affects print quality through surface roughness, stringing, inconsistent extrusion, and reduced layer adhesion, supporting dry storage and pre-drying practices to preserve material performance. What is the difference between PET vs PETG? The difference between PET and PETG lies in polymer structure, processability, and application suitability. PET is a semi‑crystalline or amorphous, but industrial PET used in bottles and packaging is often semi‑crystalline for strength and clarity. Polyethylene terephthalate polymer is used in injection molding, blow molding, and thermoforming, while PETG is a glycol-modified polyethylene terephthalate copolyester with reduced crystallinity. PETG incorporates glycol units through copolymerization with polyethylene terephthalate, disrupting molecular packing, lowering internal stress, and improving melt stability. PET exhibits higher stiffness, higher chemical resistance, and greater thermal resistance in finished products, while PET processing requires controlled industrial conditions due to crystallization behavior and dimensional shrinkage during cooling. PETG supports stable extrusion, strong layer adhesion, and low warping behavior, explaining widespread use in fused deposition modeling and functional 3D printing. PET appears frequently in bottles, food packaging, and industrial films, while PETG appears in 3D printed enclosures, protective components, medical housings, and transparent parts where impact resistance and dimensional consistency are required. Which filament is better between ABS vs PETG? PETG is generally better for casual and desktop 3D printing due to easier processing and lower shrinkage; ABS may outperform in heat resistance and stiffness where those are required. PETG provides strong impact resistance and ductile behavior while maintaining lower warping risk and reduced internal stress during cooling compared to ABS. It prints at moderate nozzle temperatures and adheres well to build surfaces without requiring fully enclosed chambers, supporting consistent print quality and improved dimensional stability under typical desktop printing conditions. ABS offers higher heat resistance and rigidity than PETG, which suits applications exposed to elevated temperatures. ABS printing involves higher nozzle and bed temperatures, greater shrinkage, and increased warping risk, complicating print reliability and dimensional control. PETG is tough and ductile, but not flexible in the way TPU or flexible filaments are, while ABS suits structural components that require higher heat resistance and rigid performance in ABS vs. PETG comparisons. What is the comparison of PETG filament properties? The comparison of PETG filament properties is shown in the table below. How does PETG Compare to PLA and ABS? PETG offers balanced performance between PLA and ABS in mechanical strength and ease of printing, but not in flexibility , it's rigid, not flexible like TPU. PETG offers better impact resistance and ductility than PLA, making it more suitable for functional parts that require toughness. PETG has lower shrinkage and warping than ABS under typical print conditions. PETG offers balanced performance compared to PLA 3D Printing Filament and ABS, with better impact resistance, lower shrinkage, and ease of printing. It provides strength and flexibility, though heat resistance is lower than ABS. What applications is PETG better suited than PLA or ABS? PETG is better suited for applications requiring durability, more ductile and impact resistant than PLA, but it is still rigid compared to flexible materials such as TPU or nylon, and moderate chemical resistance compared to PLA, while ABS offers higher heat resistance. PETG excels in producing functional parts that must withstand mechanical stress, exposure to moisture, and mild chemicals, making it ideal for protective enclosures, mechanical parts, and outdoor components where UV exposure is limited. Glycolide-modified polyethylene terephthalate filament is used to print functional parts in 3D printing because of its strength, flexibility, and moderate chemical resistance. PETG offers better toughness, heat resistance, and environmental durability, though its UV resistance is limited without stabilizers, unlike PLA 3D printing filament, which is easy to print but has low heat resistance. ABS 3D printing filament provides strength but is prone to warping and emitting fumes during printing, which can complicate the process, requiring higher nozzle and bed temperatures and more controlled printing environments. PETG provides an effective solution for applications requiring mechanical integrity, flexibility, and moderate chemical resistance in PETG vs PLA comparisons, where printability and performance under stress are important. Is PETG Flexible comparable to ABS? Yes, PETG is more flexible than ABS. PETG demonstrates higher impact resistance and greater ductility than ABS, making it more resilient to cracking or breaking under stress. PETG maintains better flexibility and resilience in applications subject to bending or mechanical stress, though its heat resistance is lower than ABS, while ABS is more rigid and offers higher heat resistance. PETG's flexibility makes it ideal for applications requiring strength and stress resistance (enclosures and components), compared to ABS 3D printing filament , which excels in high-temperature applications. How to Print PETG Successfully? To print PETG successfully, follow the five steps. First, set the bed temperature between 70 and 80°C and the nozzle temperature between 230 and 250°C for optimal extrusion, with variations depending on specific printer and material conditions. Second, use a moderate fan speed of 30-50% to cool the print and reduce warping, adjusting based on layer height and part geometry. Third, ensure first-layer adhesion by using a heated bed and applying a thin layer of adhesive or ensuring a clean, level print surface, adjusting as necessary for the printer's calibration. Fourth, adjust retraction settings to 1–2 mm for direct drive, or 4–7 mm for Bowden extruders, fine-tuning as needed based on filament diameter and extrusion settings. Lastly, maintain a print speed of 40-60 mm/s for consistent results, adjusting as needed based on print complexity and layer height. Each step ensures strong adhesion, minimal stringing, and a smooth PETG print. What are the Tips for Printing with PETG? The tips for printing with PETG are listed below. Clean the bed : Ensure the print bed is free from dust and contaminants to improve adhesion and prevent warping. Apply adhesive : Use a thin layer of glue stick to increase the first layer adhesion and prevent shifting during printing, adjusting based on the specific build surface. Adjust retraction settings : Set retraction to 1–2 mm (direct drive) or 4–7 mm (Bowden), with retraction speed of 25–45 mm/s Print first layers slowly : Slow down the print speed for the first few layers (20-30 mm/s) to ensure strong adhesion and prevent lifting, particularly on larger prints. Bed Temperature : 70-80°C. A heated bed helps prevent warping by improving adhesion during printing for the first few layers and reducing internal stress as the material cools. The temperature promotes good adhesion between layers, improving print quality and reducing the possibility of warping. The filament is used in various industries for applications (protective enclosures, mechanical components, prototypes, and outdoor parts) that need to withstand mild environmental conditions (exposure to moisture, but not extended UV exposure).
