Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 22 min read Published December 4, 2025 Updated August 26, 2026 Viscosity is the measure of a fluid’s resistance to flow. Viscosity definition indicates how thick or thin a fluid is and determines how easily it flows under an applied force. A fluid with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flows slowly, while a fluid with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, flows easily. Viscosity plays a critical role in processes (injection molding, 3D printing, and fluid transport) in manufacturing. The right viscosity ensures smooth operation, accurate mold filling, and proper material handling. Xometry understands that viscosity is essential for material selection and product design. Selecting materials with the appropriate viscosity ensures the desired flow behavior, proper adhesion, and final product quality, helping Xometry meet specific design requirements and deliver high-performance parts through manufacturing processes . Why is Viscosity Important in Fluids? Viscosity is important in fluids because it determines the internal resistance that controls how easily a substance flows under an applied force. Fluids with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, move quickly and spread easily, while fluids with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flow slowly and resist motion. The comparison between water and honey demonstrates how viscosity affects flow rate, energy transfer, and surface interaction. Industrial systems depend on viscosity control to maintain performance, reliability, and safety. Viscosity ensures a protective film between mechanical parts to minimize wear and friction under pressure in lubricants. Viscosity regulates application quality, preventing drips, sagging, or uneven spreading in paints and coatings. Engineers and manufacturers rely on precise viscosity measurements to design efficient pumps, cooling systems, and production processes where consistent flow behavior is critical. The control of viscosity ensures predictable outcomes, reduces energy losses, and supports optimal fluid performance in everyday and industrial applications. What are the Factors that Influence Viscosity? The factors that influence viscosity are listed below. Temperature : Viscosity is influenced by temperature because molecular movement changes with heat. Liquid molecules move faster as the temperature rises, reducing internal friction and lowering viscosity. Molecular motion slows at low temperatures, causing an increase in viscosity. Oil thickening during cold weather delays machinery start-up and increases energy use in industrial processes. High viscosity at low temperatures prevents proper mold filling in resin curing or injection molding, producing incomplete or defective products. Pressure : Viscosity increases with rising pressure because molecules are forced closer together, increasing resistance to flow. The effect is more pronounced in liquids with large molecular structures. High pressure can cause lubricants to thicken in manufacturing, reducing flow efficiency. Pressure adjustments are necessary to maintain consistent flow rates and prevent uneven product layers during extrusion or coating processes. Composition : The molecular structure and chemical makeup of a fluid determine its viscosity. Fluids made of large or complex molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, leading to higher viscosity. The formulation of lubricants, paints, and adhesives depends on selecting the right molecular composition to achieve stable performance in industrial production. The ratio of polymers to solvents influences flow, spread, and drying uniformity in paints and coatings. Impurities : Foreign particles or contaminants affect viscosity by disrupting molecular uniformity and increasing internal friction. The presence of solid impurities, moisture, or dissolved gases alters the balance of forces within the fluid. Impurities usually increase viscosity and can block injection nozzles in resin manufacturing. Solvent impurities cause uneven film formation, resulting in sagging, bubbles, or inconsistent finishes in coatings. “Viscosity is at the core of how fluids behave in every manufacturing process. When you understand how a material flows, fills, levels, and transfers energy, you gain control over both performance and quality. The most reliable designs start with respecting the physics of the fluid before shaping the part.” Audrius Zidonis; Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering Note from the Editor How is Viscosity Measured in Different Industries? Viscosity is measured by different industries as listed below. Automotive : Automotive industries measure viscosity in lubricants, fuels, and hydraulic fluids using rotational and capillary viscometers, along with cold-cranking simulators for low-temperature performance testing. The instruments determine how fluids behave under varying temperature and shear conditions. Accurate viscosity readings ensure that engine oils maintain flow during cold starts and provide reliable protection under high loads. Consistent viscosity prevents overheating and fluid degradation in brake and transmission systems. Automotive manufacturers rely on viscosity data for certification, quality control, and performance testing to guarantee long-term reliability. Manufacturing : Manufacturers of coatings, paints, adhesives, and resins use flow-cup (efflux time) and rotational viscometry methods. In the flow-cup method, a measured volume of liquid flows through an orifice, and the discharge time is recorded to calculate viscosity. Rotational spindle instruments apply torque at specific shear rates to measure resistance to flow. The tests maintain uniformity in spreadability, film thickness, and curing behavior. Incorrect viscosity levels cause problems (sagging, incomplete mold filling, and uneven surface finishes). Adhesive and sealant plants control viscosity to ensure consistent bonding strength, application ease, and long-term product stability. Pharmaceutica l: Pharmaceutical laboratories use rotational rheometers and capillary viscometers to evaluate the viscosity of syrups, gels, ointments, and injectable solutions. The measurement influences dosage precision, spreadability, and formulation properties that affect bioavailability. Controlled viscosity ensures stability in suspensions and prevents particle settling. Viscosity management guarantees even layering and predictable drug release during tablet coating and formulation. Pharmaceutical manufacturers test viscosity under regulated conditions to meet consistency and safety standards. Food and Beverage : Food and beverage producers measure viscosity to control texture, mouthfeel, and process flow. Instruments such as Brookfield viscometers and falling-ball viscometers assess the viscosity of sauces, creams, and beverages. Viscosity consistency maintains creaminess in dairy products, improves pour behavior in syrups, and improves coating quality in sauces. Food processors track viscosity throughout production to optimize filling, packaging, and storage stability. Polymer and Injection Molding: Polymer and injection molding industries measure the viscosity of resins and molten polymers using high-temperature capillary or rotational rheometers for controlled shear rates. The viscosity behavior at processing temperature determines how effectively the melt fills mold cavities and how uniformly it solidifies. Monitoring viscosity trends allows precise adjustment of processing parameters, improving mold filling, reducing material waste, and preventing product defects. Accurate viscosity control and material selection ensure consistent dimensional stability and surface quality in finished plastic components. What are the Methods for Measuring Viscosity in Industry? The methods for measuring viscosity in industry are listed below. Capillary : The capillary method measures viscosity by recording the time it takes for a fluid to flow through a narrow glass tube under controlled conditions. The measurement depends on tube dimensions, flow time, and fluid density. The method is exact for low- to medium-viscosity fluids (oils, solvents, and fuels). Capillary testing is used to confirm that materials meet flow and temperature performance standards in industrial settings. Quality control laboratories apply the method to detect inconsistencies in fluid formulation, ensuring stable performance during manufacturing and storage. Accurate capillary measurements improve process optimization by identifying variations in raw materials before large-scale production begins. Rotational : The rotational method involves a spindle or rotor immersed in a fluid, where torque is measured as the spindle rotates at a controlled speed. The torque indicates the internal resistance of the fluid, allowing calculation of its dynamic viscosity. The method is used for paints, coatings, adhesives, and lubricants that exhibit non-Newtonian behavior. Rotational viscometry supports quality control by monitoring shear resistance and ensuring consistency across production batches. Manufacturing facilities rely on rotational data to fine-tune mixing speeds, temperature settings, and shear conditions, preventing uneven texture, poor spreadability, or premature curing during processing. Viscometers : Industrial viscometers include instruments like flow-cups, falling-ball viscometers, and vibrating-element devices that measure flow time, fall duration, or vibration damping within a fluid. The instruments are suitable for quick production checks where rapid feedback is essential. Viscometers ensure that liquid products maintain the correct viscosity before packaging or further processing in production lines. Regular use of viscometers in manufacturing helps maintain uniformity across batches, reduce waste, and identify deviations early. Operators maintain consistent texture, stability, and appearance by using continuous viscosity data across multiple production runs. What are the Common Units of Viscosity? The common units of viscosity are listed below. SI Unit (Pa·s) : The pascal-second (Pa·s) is the standard international (SI) unit for measuring dynamic viscosity. One pascal-second corresponds to the viscosity of a fluid in which a shear stress of one pascal produces a shear rate of one reciprocal second (1 s⁻¹). Water at about 20 °C has a viscosity of 0.001 Pa·s, indicating that it flows easily. Industrial fluids such as motor oils have viscosities of 0.1 Pa·s or higher, depending on temperature and formulation. The SI unit of viscosity provides consistency in laboratory and production measurements, ensuring precision in quality control and equipment design. CGS Unit (Poise) : The poise (P) is the unit of dynamic viscosity in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system. One poise equals 0.1 Pa·s, and one centipoise (cP) equals 0.001 Pa·s. Water at 20 °C has a viscosity of about 1 cP, while motor oil ranges from 50 cP to 500 cP depending on its grade and temperature. The poise and centipoise are used in engineering and laboratory applications where fine distinctions in fluid viscosities are essential. Consistent use of the units helps manufacturers compare materials, maintain process stability, and ensure uniform fluid behavior during production and testing. How does Viscosity Affect Manufacturing Processes? Viscosity affects manufacturing processes by influencing how fluids flow, spread, coat, and fill, which in turn impacts productivity, quality, and material performance. The viscosity of coolants determines how effectively the coolants carry heat away from the cutting zone and flush out metal particles in machining operations. A moderate increase in coolant viscosity reduces flow through narrow channels, resulting in poorer heat transfer, increased tool wear, and possible thermal damage. Adhesives require a viscosity that allows the material to wet bonding surfaces and fill microscopic voids while maintaining sufficient thickness for structural strength. The adhesive traps air or fails to bond properly if the viscosity is too high, leading to premature failure. Viscosity influences how easily adhesives are mixed, pumped, and dispensed in automated systems. Coatings rely on an appropriate viscosity to enable uniform spreading, controlled film thickness, and prevention of sagging on vertical surfaces. A coating with low viscosity flows off the surface before curing, while one with high viscosity produces uneven layers or texture defects. The viscosity of the molten metal or polymer melt determines how effectively it fills mold cavities and reproduces fine features in casting or injection molding processes. A high-viscosity melt fails to reach thin sections, causing voids or incomplete fills. Viscosity affects how quickly the liquid resin flows and refills beneath each layer in resin-based 3D printing, influencing layer adhesion, print speed, and surface quality. Viscosity has direct relevance for manufacturing consistency and process optimization across all processes. Proper viscosity management ensures uniform outputs, reduces waste and rework, and supports stable process control across production runs. What are the Different Types of Viscosity? The different types of viscosity are listed below. Dynamic Viscosity : Dynamic viscosity measures the internal resistance of a fluid to shear under an applied force. The viscosity formula is defined by the equation μ = τ / γ̇, where μ is dynamic viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation between fluid layers). Dynamic viscosity is critical in industries such as lubrication, fluid transport, and hydraulics. Viscosity examples include dynamic viscosity, which ensures the fluid maintains a protective film between moving engine parts to reduce wear and friction in motor oils. Higher-viscosity oils can provide better protection at high temperatures, while lower-viscosity oils improve flow and fuel efficiency. Kinematic Viscosity : Kinematic viscosity is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to fluid density, expressed as ν = μ / ρ, where ν is kinematic viscosity, μ is dynamic viscosity, and ρ is fluid density. The property characterizes a fluid’s resistance to flow under its own weight or inertia, independent of external pressure forces. Kinematic viscosity is significant in industries (pipeline transport and coatings), where gravity and inertia influence fluid movement. For example, oil with a higher kinematic viscosity flows more slowly through pipelines, requiring more energy to pump, while in coatings, appropriate kinematic viscosity ensures uniform film formation without drips or uneven coverage. Apparent Viscosity : Apparent viscosity refers to the effective viscosity of a non-Newtonian fluid measured at a specific shear rate, temperature, or other defined condition. The formula is expressed as ηₐₚₚ = τ / γ̇, where ηₐₚₚ is apparent viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation). Apparent viscosity is used to characterize materials (adhesives, paints, and polymer melts) whose viscosity changes with shear rate during processing. For example, the apparent viscosity of a resin affects how it flows and adheres during layer deposition in 3D printing, influencing print quality and speed. What is Dynamic Viscosity? Dynamic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s internal resistance to shear under an applied force. Dynamic viscosity relates the shear stress exerted on the fluid to the resulting rate of deformation between adjacent layers. Fluid flow becomes sluggish and requires greater energy input to maintain movement when dynamic viscosity is high. Appropriate dynamic viscosity helps maintain a stable thin film of lubricant between moving parts and prevents direct metal-to-metal contact in applications such as engine lubrication, injection molding , and industrial machinery, thereby reducing wear. The lubricant film breaks down and causes damage if the dynamic viscosity is too low. The fluid does not circulate efficiently if the dynamic viscosity is too high, increasing drag, pump load, and energy consumption. What is Kinematic Viscosity? Kinematic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s inherent resistance to flow relative to its density. Kinematic viscosity is calculated by dividing a fluid’s dynamic viscosity by its density (ν = μ / ρ). A fluid's kinematic viscosity indicates how easily it moves under its own mass per unit volume compared with its internal resistance to flow. Fuel flow systems use it for consistent delivery, coolant circulation systems for reliable channel traversal, and manufacturing fluid transport processes where gravity and inertia influence throughput and stability. What is Apparent Viscosity? Apparent viscosity is the effective measure of a fluid’s resistance to shear under specific processing conditions (defined shear rate, temperature, or applied stress). Apparent viscosity describes how a fluid’s internal structure responds when adjacent layers move at different rates. Non-Newtonian fluids have a variable apparent viscosity depending on the shear rate or applied stress. For example, coatings must have a lower apparent viscosity under high shear during spraying for easy application and a higher apparent viscosity at rest to prevent sagging. Sealants require an apparent viscosity that allows them to flow into joints and then stabilize to remain in place. Apparent viscosity determines how readily the material flows under high shear during extrusion and how well it maintains shape after exiting the die in polymer extrusion. Proper control of apparent viscosity ensures uniform products, efficient processing, and minimal defects in manufacturing. How does Viscosity Affect Injection Molding Processes? Viscosity affects the injection molding process by determining how easily the resin flows into the mold, how it cools, and the final part quality. High-viscosity resins flow more slowly, which leads to incomplete filling or short shots in intricate or thin-walled sections. Higher injection pressures are required, which increases overall cycle time. Resins with excessively low viscosity can leak into parting lines, create flash, or reduce dimensional accuracy. Proper viscosity ensures that the mold fills, cools evenly, and produces parts with smooth surfaces, minimal sink marks, and strong weld lines. Expertise in material selection helps balance viscosity for optimal mold filling, cooling, and part quality. How does Viscosity Impact Extrusion Processes? Viscosity impacts polymer extrusion by governing how the melt flows, stabilizes, and forms the final product dimensions. High-viscosity melts resist flow, requiring more force to push material through the screw and die, which reduces production rates. Lower-viscosity melts flow more easily and increase throughput, but lead to unstable flow, uneven wall thickness, or surface defects. Fluctuations in melt viscosity in non-Newtonian polymers cause pressure variations that affect dimensional consistency and product quality. Precise control of viscosity ensures uniform die filling, consistent cross-sections, and proper cooling. Real-time monitoring of melt viscosity allows adjustments to screw speed, temperature, and back-pressure, making viscosity a critical factor for quality control and process optimization in extrusion. What is the Importance of Viscosity in Casting? The importance of viscosity in casting is listed below. Flow into Mold Cavities : Viscosity determines how easily molten metal or ceramic slurry penetrates mold geometry. High viscosity or insufficiently heated metal prevents full filling of thin sections, leading to voids or incomplete castings. Defect Prevention : Maintaining proper viscosity reduces defects such as porosity, surface roughness, and, in investment casting, shell cracking and incomplete shell formation. Stable viscosity ensures uniform shell thickness and reliable strength. Die Casting Relevance : The molten alloy must flow rapidly into the mold before solidification begins in die casting. Lower viscosity improves mold filling, reduces cold shuts, and increases part quality. Investment Casting Relevance : The viscosity of the ceramic slurry affects coating layers on the wax pattern, shell integrity, and final casting accuracy in investment casting. Maintaining optimal viscosity ensures proper coating, mold strength, and dimensional precision. How does Viscosity Influence 3D Printing (Additive Manufacturing)? Viscosity influences 3D printing processes by governing how well the material flows, how each layer adheres, and how the final structure maintains its shape. Stereolithography (SLA) requires low-viscosity resin to refill the tank rapidly between layers, reduce trapped air or voids, and enable fine feature resolution. The viscosity of molten polymer affects flow through the nozzle, filament bonding, and layer consistency, directly impacting print precision, strength, and quality in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). Powder-bed processes such as Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) depend on the flow behavior of the partially melted powder to ensure particles coalesce properly, which affects density, mechanical strength, and dimensional accuracy. Proper control of viscosity across the processes ensures high print precision, strong interlayer adhesion, and superior structural integrity in printed parts. Why is Viscosity Important in Coatings and Paint Formulations? Viscosity is essential in coatings and paint formulations because it controls how the liquid flows onto and adheres to a surface. Proper viscosity improves sprayability, film formation, and drying behavior in industrial paints and powder coatings. Low viscosity increases atomization during spray application, permitting fine mist formation and even coverage. High viscosity supports a thicker film build without sagging on vertical surfaces, provided it remains within the application range. Maintaining optimal viscosity in paint lines ensures a consistent surface finish, accurate film thickness, and defect-free drying. Powder coatings benefit from controlling melt viscosity during curing to ensure proper flow, leveling, and uniform protective layers. Insufficient viscosity control results in uneven coatings, runs, orange peel texture, and reduced durability of the finished product. How does Viscosity Affect the Performance of Adhesives and Sealants? Viscosity affects the performance of adhesives and sealants by controlling how well the material flows, wets the substrate, and forms a strong bond, and how easily it is applied. Proper viscosity ensures the adhesive penetrates surface irregularities and establishes intimate contact between surfaces. Lower viscosity adhesives flow readily, filling micro‑voids on rough or porous surfaces and improving bond strength. Higher viscosity adhesives remain in place under gravity or vertical orientation, preserving joint thickness and preventing sagging or dripping during application. The viscosity of epoxy resins influences mixing, dispensing, and layer uniformity, affecting cohesive strength upon curing. Sealant viscosity determines how well the material extrudes into joints and gaps and how well it resists movement under load after curing. Deviations from the optimal viscosity range reduce bond strength, impair gap-filling, or compromise joint integrity. Why Do Lubricants in Machining Depend on Viscosity? Lubricants in machining depend on viscosity because it determines the thickness of the protective film between moving parts, reducing wear, friction, and heat generation. Correct viscosity ensures the film remains stable under load, preventing metal‑to‑metal contact. The lubricant is unable to form a sufficient film if the viscosity is too low, increasing friction and wear. Excessively high viscosity impedes fluid flow and reduces cooling efficiency, increasing localized heat. Viscosity influences chip removal and tool friction in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining by controlling how well the lubricant or coolant reaches the cutting interface. Proper viscosity ensures adequate lubrication of critical components in automotive engines, increasing performance and prolonging engine life. What are Real-World Applications of Viscosity in Manufacturing? The real-world applications of viscosity in manufacturing are listed below. Automotive : Viscosity determines how lubricants flow in engines, how fuel is injected and sprayed, and how sealants cure on body panels. Proper viscosity ensures reliable component performance, reduces wear, and supports tight tolerances in drivetrain and chassis systems. Xometry’s Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining and 3D printing services allow for precision manufacturing of automotive components where viscosity-controlled fluids or coatings are required. Aerospace : Viscosity affects coatings on airframes and turbines, adhesive bonding in composite assemblies, and hydraulic fluid behavior in flight control systems. Controlling viscosity delivers consistent surface finish, durable bonds, and stable fluid performance under temperature and pressure extremes. Xometry provides aerospace-grade materials and precision machining to meet the exacting standards for aerospace components requiring specific viscosity ranges in fluids and coatings. Medical : Viscosity impacts the formulation of syringes, fluid delivery systems, and biocompatible adhesives. Accurate viscosity control ensures correct flow in micro‑channels, layer printing in implant manufacturing, and consistent material behavior in sterile environments. Xometry’s services (custom injection molding and 3D printing) support the medical industry’s need for high-quality, precise parts where viscosity is important in fluid handling and material consistency. Chemical : Viscosity influences mixing, pumping, and coating of chemical slurries, resins, and polymer melts. Viscosity must remain within range to prevent blockages in process lines, maintain productivity, and ensure uniform product quality across batches. Xometry’s manufacturing processes (injection molding and CNC machining) ensure precision control in producing components that require specific viscosity tolerances for reliable performance in chemical industries. Food : Viscosity shapes how sauces, creams, and liquids flow through filling machines, coat surfaces, and deliver mouthfeel. Controlled viscosity ensures stable processing, predictable production rates, and consistent consumer experience. Xometry’s services (3D printing and injection molding) provide custom solutions for food packaging and dispensing systems, where precise viscosity is essential to maintaining quality and performance. How does Viscosity Affect Fluid Transport Systems? Viscosity influences fluid transport systems by determining flow resistance, pressure drop, energy consumption, and system design regulation. Higher viscosity leads to greater internal friction and slower fluid movement, which demands higher pumping power and increased operational cost. Fluid transport lines carrying viscous liquids require appropriately rated pumps, larger pipe diameters, and accurate temperature control to maintain target flow rates and avoid issues (cavitation or blockages). Effective viscosity management enables consistent flow velocity, stable delivery of process fluids, and precise system performance in manufacturing pipelines and transfer networks. First, measure the viscosity of ingredients (sauces, creams, or beverages) to determine their flow characteristics and set appropriate processing parameters. Second, adjust temperature and ingredient concentrations to achieve the desired viscosity, ensuring proper flow during manufacturing while maintaining consistent texture and mouthfeel. Third, control viscosity during transportation through pipes and filling systems to prevent clogging, ensure even flow, and minimize splashing or foaming. Lastly, perform regular quality control checks to verify that viscosity remains within the target range, maintaining uniformity and product quality throughout production. Water's uniform response to temperature, wide availability in pure form, and consistent flow behavior make it a reliable benchmark for comparing the viscosity of other liquids. Using water as a reference allows researchers and engineers to evaluate whether a fluid flows more easily or more slowly relative to the standard, facilitating consistent measurement and comparison of fluid viscosities. Viscosity defines the internal friction that influences whether a flow remains smooth or becomes turbulent. High viscosity reduces flow velocity and stabilizes the motion of fluid layers, promoting laminar flow where energy loss through friction is predictable. Low viscosity encourages faster movement and turbulence, leading to irregular flow patterns and greater energy dissipation. Viscosity determines how much pressure is needed to move a fluid through a pipeline in fluid transport systems. Engineers design pipe diameters, pump capacities, and flow rates based on viscosity to maintain efficient flow while minimizing energy loss. The balance between viscosity, velocity, and pipe geometry governs Reynolds number, an important indicator of whether the flow is laminar or turbulent in fluid mechanics. Density measures the mass of a substance per unit volume, indicating how much matter is contained in a given space. Viscosity affects how fluids flow through pipes, machinery, and lubrication systems, influencing pumping resistance and energy requirements. Density affects fluid weight, hydrostatic pressure, and buoyancy, which are critical in storage, transport, and separation processes. Viscosity governs injection and lubrication performance in fuel systems, while density contributes to overall fuel mass and pressure distribution, influencing combustion efficiency. Viscosity and density are essential in engineering and process design, as the two govern flow behavior, energy efficiency, and system performance across industrial applications. Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 22 min read Published December 4, 2025 Updated August 26, 2026 Viscosity is the measure of a fluid’s resistance to flow. Viscosity definition indicates how thick or thin a fluid is and determines how easily it flows under an applied force. A fluid with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flows slowly, while a fluid with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, flows easily. Viscosity plays a critical role in processes (injection molding, 3D printing, and fluid transport) in manufacturing. The right viscosity ensures smooth operation, accurate mold filling, and proper material handling. Xometry understands that viscosity is essential for material selection and product design. Selecting materials with the appropriate viscosity ensures the desired flow behavior, proper adhesion, and final product quality, helping Xometry meet specific design requirements and deliver high-performance parts through manufacturing processes . Why is Viscosity Important in Fluids? Viscosity is important in fluids because it determines the internal resistance that controls how easily a substance flows under an applied force. Fluids with low viscosity<dynamic-value> water, move quickly and spread easily, while fluids with high viscosity<dynamic-value> honey, flow slowly and resist motion. The comparison between water and honey demonstrates how viscosity affects flow rate, energy transfer, and surface interaction. Industrial systems depend on viscosity control to maintain performance, reliability, and safety. Viscosity ensures a protective film between mechanical parts to minimize wear and friction under pressure in lubricants. Viscosity regulates application quality, preventing drips, sagging, or uneven spreading in paints and coatings. Engineers and manufacturers rely on precise viscosity measurements to design efficient pumps, cooling systems, and production processes where consistent flow behavior is critical. The control of viscosity ensures predictable outcomes, reduces energy losses, and supports optimal fluid performance in everyday and industrial applications. What are the Factors that Influence Viscosity? The factors that influence viscosity are listed below. Temperature : Viscosity is influenced by temperature because molecular movement changes with heat. Liquid molecules move faster as the temperature rises, reducing internal friction and lowering viscosity. Molecular motion slows at low temperatures, causing an increase in viscosity. Oil thickening during cold weather delays machinery start-up and increases energy use in industrial processes. High viscosity at low temperatures prevents proper mold filling in resin curing or injection molding, producing incomplete or defective products. Pressure : Viscosity increases with rising pressure because molecules are forced closer together, increasing resistance to flow. The effect is more pronounced in liquids with large molecular structures. High pressure can cause lubricants to thicken in manufacturing, reducing flow efficiency. Pressure adjustments are necessary to maintain consistent flow rates and prevent uneven product layers during extrusion or coating processes. Composition : The molecular structure and chemical makeup of a fluid determine its viscosity. Fluids made of large or complex molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, leading to higher viscosity. The formulation of lubricants, paints, and adhesives depends on selecting the right molecular composition to achieve stable performance in industrial production. The ratio of polymers to solvents influences flow, spread, and drying uniformity in paints and coatings. Impurities : Foreign particles or contaminants affect viscosity by disrupting molecular uniformity and increasing internal friction. The presence of solid impurities, moisture, or dissolved gases alters the balance of forces within the fluid. Impurities usually increase viscosity and can block injection nozzles in resin manufacturing. Solvent impurities cause uneven film formation, resulting in sagging, bubbles, or inconsistent finishes in coatings. “Viscosity is at the core of how fluids behave in every manufacturing process. When you understand how a material flows, fills, levels, and transfers energy, you gain control over both performance and quality. The most reliable designs start with respecting the physics of the fluid before shaping the part.” Audrius Zidonis; Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering Note from the Editor How is Viscosity Measured in Different Industries? Viscosity is measured by different industries as listed below. Automotive : Automotive industries measure viscosity in lubricants, fuels, and hydraulic fluids using rotational and capillary viscometers, along with cold-cranking simulators for low-temperature performance testing. The instruments determine how fluids behave under varying temperature and shear conditions. Accurate viscosity readings ensure that engine oils maintain flow during cold starts and provide reliable protection under high loads. Consistent viscosity prevents overheating and fluid degradation in brake and transmission systems. Automotive manufacturers rely on viscosity data for certification, quality control, and performance testing to guarantee long-term reliability. Manufacturing : Manufacturers of coatings, paints, adhesives, and resins use flow-cup (efflux time) and rotational viscometry methods. In the flow-cup method, a measured volume of liquid flows through an orifice, and the discharge time is recorded to calculate viscosity. Rotational spindle instruments apply torque at specific shear rates to measure resistance to flow. The tests maintain uniformity in spreadability, film thickness, and curing behavior. Incorrect viscosity levels cause problems (sagging, incomplete mold filling, and uneven surface finishes). Adhesive and sealant plants control viscosity to ensure consistent bonding strength, application ease, and long-term product stability. Pharmaceutica l: Pharmaceutical laboratories use rotational rheometers and capillary viscometers to evaluate the viscosity of syrups, gels, ointments, and injectable solutions. The measurement influences dosage precision, spreadability, and formulation properties that affect bioavailability. Controlled viscosity ensures stability in suspensions and prevents particle settling. Viscosity management guarantees even layering and predictable drug release during tablet coating and formulation. Pharmaceutical manufacturers test viscosity under regulated conditions to meet consistency and safety standards. Food and Beverage : Food and beverage producers measure viscosity to control texture, mouthfeel, and process flow. Instruments such as Brookfield viscometers and falling-ball viscometers assess the viscosity of sauces, creams, and beverages. Viscosity consistency maintains creaminess in dairy products, improves pour behavior in syrups, and improves coating quality in sauces. Food processors track viscosity throughout production to optimize filling, packaging, and storage stability. Polymer and Injection Molding: Polymer and injection molding industries measure the viscosity of resins and molten polymers using high-temperature capillary or rotational rheometers for controlled shear rates. The viscosity behavior at processing temperature determines how effectively the melt fills mold cavities and how uniformly it solidifies. Monitoring viscosity trends allows precise adjustment of processing parameters, improving mold filling, reducing material waste, and preventing product defects. Accurate viscosity control and material selection ensure consistent dimensional stability and surface quality in finished plastic components. What are the Methods for Measuring Viscosity in Industry? The methods for measuring viscosity in industry are listed below. Capillary : The capillary method measures viscosity by recording the time it takes for a fluid to flow through a narrow glass tube under controlled conditions. The measurement depends on tube dimensions, flow time, and fluid density. The method is exact for low- to medium-viscosity fluids (oils, solvents, and fuels). Capillary testing is used to confirm that materials meet flow and temperature performance standards in industrial settings. Quality control laboratories apply the method to detect inconsistencies in fluid formulation, ensuring stable performance during manufacturing and storage. Accurate capillary measurements improve process optimization by identifying variations in raw materials before large-scale production begins. Rotational : The rotational method involves a spindle or rotor immersed in a fluid, where torque is measured as the spindle rotates at a controlled speed. The torque indicates the internal resistance of the fluid, allowing calculation of its dynamic viscosity. The method is used for paints, coatings, adhesives, and lubricants that exhibit non-Newtonian behavior. Rotational viscometry supports quality control by monitoring shear resistance and ensuring consistency across production batches. Manufacturing facilities rely on rotational data to fine-tune mixing speeds, temperature settings, and shear conditions, preventing uneven texture, poor spreadability, or premature curing during processing. Viscometers : Industrial viscometers include instruments like flow-cups, falling-ball viscometers, and vibrating-element devices that measure flow time, fall duration, or vibration damping within a fluid. The instruments are suitable for quick production checks where rapid feedback is essential. Viscometers ensure that liquid products maintain the correct viscosity before packaging or further processing in production lines. Regular use of viscometers in manufacturing helps maintain uniformity across batches, reduce waste, and identify deviations early. Operators maintain consistent texture, stability, and appearance by using continuous viscosity data across multiple production runs. What are the Common Units of Viscosity? The common units of viscosity are listed below. SI Unit (Pa·s) : The pascal-second (Pa·s) is the standard international (SI) unit for measuring dynamic viscosity. One pascal-second corresponds to the viscosity of a fluid in which a shear stress of one pascal produces a shear rate of one reciprocal second (1 s⁻¹). Water at about 20 °C has a viscosity of 0.001 Pa·s, indicating that it flows easily. Industrial fluids such as motor oils have viscosities of 0.1 Pa·s or higher, depending on temperature and formulation. The SI unit of viscosity provides consistency in laboratory and production measurements, ensuring precision in quality control and equipment design. CGS Unit (Poise) : The poise (P) is the unit of dynamic viscosity in the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system. One poise equals 0.1 Pa·s, and one centipoise (cP) equals 0.001 Pa·s. Water at 20 °C has a viscosity of about 1 cP, while motor oil ranges from 50 cP to 500 cP depending on its grade and temperature. The poise and centipoise are used in engineering and laboratory applications where fine distinctions in fluid viscosities are essential. Consistent use of the units helps manufacturers compare materials, maintain process stability, and ensure uniform fluid behavior during production and testing. Viscosity affects manufacturing processes by influencing how fluids flow, spread, coat, and fill, which in turn impacts productivity, quality, and material performance. The viscosity of coolants determines how effectively the coolants carry heat away from the cutting zone and flush out metal particles in machining operations. A moderate increase in coolant viscosity reduces flow through narrow channels, resulting in poorer heat transfer, increased tool wear, and possible thermal damage. Adhesives require a viscosity that allows the material to wet bonding surfaces and fill microscopic voids while maintaining sufficient thickness for structural strength. The adhesive traps air or fails to bond properly if the viscosity is too high, leading to premature failure. Viscosity influences how easily adhesives are mixed, pumped, and dispensed in automated systems. Coatings rely on an appropriate viscosity to enable uniform spreading, controlled film thickness, and prevention of sagging on vertical surfaces. A coating with low viscosity flows off the surface before curing, while one with high viscosity produces uneven layers or texture defects. The viscosity of the molten metal or polymer melt determines how effectively it fills mold cavities and reproduces fine features in casting or injection molding processes. A high-viscosity melt fails to reach thin sections, causing voids or incomplete fills. Viscosity affects how quickly the liquid resin flows and refills beneath each layer in resin-based 3D printing, influencing layer adhesion, print speed, and surface quality. Viscosity has direct relevance for manufacturing consistency and process optimization across all processes. Proper viscosity management ensures uniform outputs, reduces waste and rework, and supports stable process control across production runs. What are the Different Types of Viscosity? The different types of viscosity are listed below. Dynamic Viscosity : Dynamic viscosity measures the internal resistance of a fluid to shear under an applied force. The viscosity formula is defined by the equation μ = τ / γ̇, where μ is dynamic viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation between fluid layers). Dynamic viscosity is critical in industries such as lubrication, fluid transport, and hydraulics. Viscosity examples include dynamic viscosity, which ensures the fluid maintains a protective film between moving engine parts to reduce wear and friction in motor oils. Higher-viscosity oils can provide better protection at high temperatures, while lower-viscosity oils improve flow and fuel efficiency. Kinematic Viscosity : Kinematic viscosity is the ratio of dynamic viscosity to fluid density, expressed as ν = μ / ρ, where ν is kinematic viscosity, μ is dynamic viscosity, and ρ is fluid density. The property characterizes a fluid’s resistance to flow under its own weight or inertia, independent of external pressure forces. Kinematic viscosity is significant in industries (pipeline transport and coatings), where gravity and inertia influence fluid movement. For example, oil with a higher kinematic viscosity flows more slowly through pipelines, requiring more energy to pump, while in coatings, appropriate kinematic viscosity ensures uniform film formation without drips or uneven coverage. Apparent Viscosity : Apparent viscosity refers to the effective viscosity of a non-Newtonian fluid measured at a specific shear rate, temperature, or other defined condition. The formula is expressed as ηₐₚₚ = τ / γ̇, where ηₐₚₚ is apparent viscosity, τ is shear stress (force per unit area), and γ̇ is shear rate (rate of deformation). Apparent viscosity is used to characterize materials (adhesives, paints, and polymer melts) whose viscosity changes with shear rate during processing. For example, the apparent viscosity of a resin affects how it flows and adheres during layer deposition in 3D printing, influencing print quality and speed. What is Dynamic Viscosity? Dynamic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s internal resistance to shear under an applied force. Dynamic viscosity relates the shear stress exerted on the fluid to the resulting rate of deformation between adjacent layers. Fluid flow becomes sluggish and requires greater energy input to maintain movement when dynamic viscosity is high. Appropriate dynamic viscosity helps maintain a stable thin film of lubricant between moving parts and prevents direct metal-to-metal contact in applications such as engine lubrication, injection molding , and industrial machinery, thereby reducing wear. The lubricant film breaks down and causes damage if the dynamic viscosity is too low. The fluid does not circulate efficiently if the dynamic viscosity is too high, increasing drag, pump load, and energy consumption. What is Kinematic Viscosity? Kinematic viscosity is a measure of a fluid’s inherent resistance to flow relative to its density. Kinematic viscosity is calculated by dividing a fluid’s dynamic viscosity by its density (ν = μ / ρ). A fluid's kinematic viscosity indicates how easily it moves under its own mass per unit volume compared with its internal resistance to flow. Fuel flow systems use it for consistent delivery, coolant circulation systems for reliable channel traversal, and manufacturing fluid transport processes where gravity and inertia influence throughput and stability. Lower viscosity improves mold filling, reduces cold shuts, and increases part quality. The viscosity of molten polymer affects flow through the nozzle, filament bonding, and layer consistency, directly impacting print precision, strength, and quality in Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM). Powder-bed processes such as Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) depend on the flow behavior of the partially melted powder to ensure particles coalesce properly, which affects density, mechanical strength, and dimensional accuracy. Proper control of viscosity across the processes ensures high print precision, strong interlayer adhesion, and superior structural integrity in printed parts. Proper viscosity improves sprayability, film formation, and drying behavior in industrial paints and powder coatings. Low viscosity increases atomization during spray application, permitting fine mist formation and even coverage. High viscosity supports a thicker film build without sagging on vertical surfaces, provided it remains within the application range. Maintaining optimal viscosity in paint lines ensures a consistent surface finish, accurate film thickness, and defect-free drying. Powder coatings benefit from controlling melt viscosity during curing to ensure proper flow, leveling, and uniform protective layers. Sealant viscosity determines how well the material extrudes into joints and gaps and how well it resists movement under load after curing. Deviations from the optimal viscosity range reduce bond strength, impair gap-filling, or compromise joint integrity. Why Do Lubricants in Machining Depend on Viscosity? Correct viscosity ensures the film remains stable under load, preventing metal‑to‑metal contact. The lubricant is unable to form a sufficient film if the viscosity is too low, increasing friction and wear. Excessively high viscosity impedes fluid flow and reduces cooling efficiency, increasing localized heat. Viscosity influences chip removal and tool friction in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining by controlling how well the lubricant or coolant reaches the cutting interface. Proper viscosity ensures adequate lubrication of critical components in automotive engines, increasing performance and prolonging engine life. Proper viscosity ensures reliable component performance, reduces wear, and supports tight tolerances in drivetrain and chassis systems. events.before: Resources / Sheet / Understanding Sheet Metal Tolerances Understanding Sheet Metal Tolerances Written by Greg Paulsen 2 min read Published October 6, 2020 Updated August 21, 2026 Check out our list of quick tips and tolerance specifications for designing Sheet Metal countersinks, curls, and hems! A Quick Guide to Countersinks, Curls, and Hems Compared to other machining processes, designing Sheet Metal parts is relatively straight-forward. Sheet metal parts are made from a single metal sheet by punching, cutting, stamping, and/or bending and are known for their end-use durability. But there are still many important design-for-manufacturability issues to consider. Check out our list of quick tips and tolerance specifications for designing Sheet Metal countersinks, curls, and hems! And for even more information, download our free Sheet Metal Design Guide ! Countersinks The maximum depth of a countersink is .6 times the material thickness of the part. Countersinks must be at least 8 times the material thickness from each other, 4 times the material’s thickness from an edge, and 3 times the material’s thickness from a bend. Curls Outside radius of curls must be at least 2 times the material’s thickness. Holes should be placed away from the curl at least a distance of the radius of the curl plus the material’s thickness. BGA Assembly Capabilities When it comes to BGA assembly, let's first understand what BGA is. BGAs (Ball Grid Arrays) are a type of IC package where the pins are placed in the form of solder balls. Compared to traditional packaging technologies such as DIP (Dual In-line Package) or QFP (Quad Flat Package), BGA employs a higher-density pin layout. With technological advancements, there is an increasing demand in PCB design for complex and small-sized chips. These chips enable higher integration and functionality within smaller spaces. Hence, there is a need for a packaging method that can accommodate these chips with higher I/O density while maintaining cost-effectiveness. BGA (Ball Grid Array) is precisely such a packaging method that meets these requirements. What is BGA Assembly? BGA assembly refers to the process of mounting a Ball Grid Array (BGA) onto a PCB using the reflow soldering technique. BGA is a surface-mounted component that utilizes an array of solder balls for electrical interconnection. As the circuit board passes through a solder reflow oven, these solder balls melt, forming electrical connections. Steps of BGA Assembly The BGA assembly process typically involves the following steps: PCB Preparation: The PCB is prepared by applying solder paste to the pads where the BGA will be mounted. The solder paste is a mixture of solder alloy particles and flux, which helps with the soldering process. Placement of BGAs: The BGAs, which consist of the integrated circuit chip with solder balls on the bottom, are placed onto the prepared PCB. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. BGA assembly service is one of the many service types we offer. PCBWay can provide you with high-quality and cost-effective BGA assembly for your PCBs. The minimum pitch for BGA assembly that we can accommodate is 0.25mm 0.3mm . PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - M5StackChan AI Desktop Robot Can AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly in ADC PCB Design? SMT Assembly Capabilities What is SMT Assembly? SMT, which stands for Surface Mount Technology, is a method of directly mounting electronic components onto the surface of a PCB. This method is commonly used for installing Surface Mount Devices (SMDs), which have smaller pins or are pinless in structure. Compared to traditional through-hole technology, SMT provides higher levels of automated manufacturing capabilities, reduces costs, and improves quality. Additionally, SMT allows for the installation of more components on a limited PCB board area. Through-hole technology is typically used for components such as large transformers and high-power heat-dissipating semiconductors that are not suitable for surface mounting. SMT components have smaller leads or no leads at all, and common structures include short pins or leads, flat contacts, and Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs). PCBWay SMT Assembly Capability Overview We have the capabilities to assemble SMT prototype PCBs in small production runs with manual and/or automated SMT production processes, including single- or double-sided component insertions. Our production facilities can assemble the following SMT types: Ball Grid Array (BGA) Ultra-Fine Ball Grid Array (uBGA) Quad Flat Pack No-Lead (QFN) Quad Flat Package (QFP) Small Outline Integrated Circuit (SOIC) Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier (PLCC) Package-On-Package (PoP) Small Chip Packages (0.2mm pitch ) Main SMT Machines in PCBWay Automatic Solder Paste Printer Reflow Soldering Machine Pick & Place Machine Inspection equipment (3D SPI machine, online AOI machine, offline AOI machine, X-Ray machine) SMT Manufacturing Process SMT Process Flow Chart PCB, SMC, Stencil Preparation and Examination Prepare the PCB, surface-mount components, and stencil, and inspect them for any defects. Solder Paste Printing The solder paste screen printing machine used for SMT is required to print solder paste onto the PCB before surface-mount components undergo reflow soldering. 3D Solder Paste Inspection The solder paste printing process is one of the most critical stages in SMT assembly. The earlier the defects are identified, the lower the cost of correcting them. To ensure defect-free solder paste deposition in the required quantity, it is recommended to perform a comprehensive inspection of each printed PCB before commencing component placement. 3D solder paste inspection not only checks the coverage area and short circuits of the solder paste but also accurately measures the shape and volume of the solder deposits. On the other hand, 2D solder paste inspection cannot assess the volume or shape of the solder deposition. Pick & Place The SMT pick and place machine is one of the most crucial equipments in surface mount technology. It is also referred to as the pick-and-place robot. Prior to soldering, it picks up SMDs and places them onto the PCB. Reflow Soldering Reflow Oven: After the surface mount components are placed, the PCB is sent into the reflow oven. Preheat Zone: The first zone in the reflow oven is the preheat zone, where the temperature of the PCB and all components gradually increases simultaneously. The heating rate in this stage is 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches 140°C-160°C. Soaking Zone: The PCB remains at a temperature of 140°C-160°C for a soaking period of 60-90 seconds. Reflow Zone: The circuit board then enters a peak temperature zone where the temperature rises at a rate of 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches a peak of 210°C-230°C. This melts the solder in the solder paste, bonding the component leads to the solder pads on the PCB. The surface tension of the molten solder helps to hold the components in place. Cooling Zone: In the cooling zone, the heated PCB and components gradually cool down, allowing the solder joints to solidify and stabilize. The cooling process is critical for the formation of solder joints and securing the components. It helps ensure the reliability and mechanical strength of the solder joints. If the circuit board is double-sided, the printing, placement, and reflow process can be repeated using solder paste or adhesive to secure the components in place. AOI Machine Inspection After the soldering process, professional quality inspectors will perform AOI on the circuit boards to check for any defects before the products are stored in the warehouse. SMT, which stands for Surface Mount Technology, is a method of directly mounting electronic components onto the surface of a PCB. This method is commonly used for installing Surface Mount Devices (SMDs), which have smaller pins or are pinless in structure. Compared to traditional through-hole technology, SMT provides higher levels of automated manufacturing capabilities, reduces costs, and improves quality. Additionally, SMT allows for the installation of more components on a limited PCB board area. Through-hole technology is typically used for components such as large transformers and high-power heat-dissipating semiconductors that are not suitable for surface mounting. SMT components have smaller leads or no leads at all, and common structures include short pins or leads, flat contacts, and Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs). PCBWay SMT Assembly Capability Overview We have the capabilities to assemble SMT prototype PCBs in small production runs with manual and/or automated SMT production processes, including single- or double-sided component insertions. Our production facilities can assemble the following SMT types: Ball Grid Array (BGA) Ultra-Fine Ball Grid Array (uBGA) Quad Flat Pack No-Lead (QFN) Quad Flat Package (QFP) Small Outline Integrated Circuit (SOIC) Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier (PLCC) Package-On-Package (PoP) Small Chip Packages (0.2mm pitch ) Main SMT Machines in PCBWay Automatic Solder Paste Printer Reflow Soldering Machine Pick & Place Machine Inspection equipment (3D SPI machine, online AOI machine, offline AOI machine, X-Ray machine) SMT Manufacturing Process SMT Process Flow Chart PCB, SMC, Stencil Preparation and Examination Prepare the PCB, surface-mount components, and stencil, and inspect them for any defects. Solder Paste Printing The solder paste screen printing machine used for SMT is required to print solder paste onto the PCB before surface-mount components undergo reflow soldering. 3D Solder Paste Inspection The solder paste printing process is one of the most critical stages in SMT assembly. The earlier the defects are identified, the lower the cost of correcting them. To ensure defect-free solder paste deposition in the required quantity, it is recommended to perform a comprehensive inspection of each printed PCB before commencing component placement. 3D solder paste inspection not only checks the coverage area and short circuits of the solder paste but also accurately measures the shape and volume of the solder deposits. On the other hand, 2D solder paste inspection cannot assess the volume or shape of the solder deposition. Pick & Place The SMT pick and place machine is one of the most crucial equipments in surface mount technology. It is also referred to as the pick-and-place robot. Prior to soldering, it picks up SMDs and places them onto the PCB. Reflow Soldering Reflow Oven: After the surface mount components are placed, the PCB is sent into the reflow oven. Preheat Zone: The first zone in the reflow oven is the preheat zone, where the temperature of the PCB and all components gradually increases simultaneously. The heating rate in this stage is 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches 140°C-160°C. Soaking Zone: The PCB remains at a temperature of 140°C-160°C for a soaking period of 60-90 seconds. Reflow Zone: The circuit board then enters a peak temperature zone where the temperature rises at a rate of 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches a peak of 210°C-230°C. This melts the solder in the solder paste, bonding the component leads to the solder pads on the PCB. The surface tension of the molten solder helps to hold the components in place. Cooling Zone: In the cooling zone, the heated PCB and components gradually cool down, allowing the solder joints to solidify and stabilize. The cooling process is critical for the formation of solder joints and securing the components. It helps ensure the reliability and mechanical strength of the solder joints. If the circuit board is double-sided, the printing, placement, and reflow process can be repeated using solder paste or adhesive to secure the components in place. AOI Machine Inspection After the soldering process, professional quality inspectors will perform AOI on the circuit boards to check for any defects before the products are stored in the warehouse. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Digital Light Processing (DLP) Overview Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview:What Is a DLP 3D Printer? How Do DLP 3D Printers Work? Digital Light Processing is a 3d printing process where a projector is used to cure photopolymer resin. Very similar to SLA where the only difference is that instead of a UV laser to cure the photopolymer resin, a safelight (light bulb) is used. Objects are created the same as SLA with the object being either pulled out of the resin which creates space for the uncured resin at the bottom of the container and to form the next layer of the object or down into the tank with the next layer being cured on the top. A diagram illustrated the DLP setup. Source: DruckWege.de Objects that are printed with Digital Light Processing have less visible layers versus other processes such as FDM/FFF. Compared with SLA, DLP can have faster build speeds due to a single layer being created in one singular digital image whereas with SLA, the UV laser has to scan the vat with a single point (trace out the object layer). Also, the same photopolymer resins that can be used with SLA, can be used for DLP 3D Printing. Objects printed with this process have the same strengths and weaknesses. Similar to SLA, DLP is commonly used to generate highly detailed artwork, non-functional prototypes, and can be used to make molds in investment casting applications. Main DLP 3D Printing Technologies Digital Light Processing provides excellent capabilities for 3D printing / Additive Manufacturing processes with an eye on efficiency. DLP is your go-to method when opting for a quick printing process without compromising on the quality of intricate parts. Just like their SLA counterparts, desktop DLP 3D printers are built around a resin tank with transparent bottom and a build platform that descends into a resin tank to create parts upside down, layer by layer. The difference is the light source. DLP 3D printers use a digital projector screen to flash an image of a layer across the entire platform, curing all points simultaneously.Now that you know how SLA works, it’s time to take a closer look at DLP. DLP is a “sister technology” to SLA as the only big difference is the light source used to cure the resin. As we just mentioned, SLA printers use lasers combined with galvanometers to cure resin. With a DLP 3D printer, the light source is a specially developed digital light projector screen. Thanks to this screen, DLP is generally considered to be faster than SLA, and here’s why: With SLA, the laser has to individually cure the resin in a “point to point” technique. On the other hand, a DLP projector screen flashes an image of a layer all at once! Thus all points of a layer can be cured simultaneously. In this way, the print speed is increased in comparison to SLA since it takes less time to cure a single layer. Since the DLP is a digital technology, the 2D image that is projected is composed of pixels. When translated into three dimensions, they become voxels. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Digital Light Processing (DLP) Overview Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview:What Is a DLP 3D Printer? How Do DLP 3D Printers Work? Digital Light Processing is a 3d printing process where a projector is used to cure photopolymer resin. Very similar to SLA where the only difference is that instead of a UV laser to cure the photopolymer resin, a safelight (light bulb) is used. Objects are created the same as SLA with the object being either pulled out of the resin which creates space for the uncured resin at the bottom of the container and to form the next layer of the object or down into the tank with the next layer being cured on the top. A diagram illustrated the DLP setup. Source: DruckWege.de Objects that are printed with Digital Light Processing have less visible layers versus other processes such as FDM/FFF. Compared with SLA, DLP can have faster build speeds due to a single layer being created in one singular digital image whereas with SLA, the UV laser has to scan the vat with a single point (trace out the object layer). Also, the same photopolymer resins that can be used with SLA, can be used for DLP 3D Printing. Objects printed with this process have the same strengths and weaknesses. Similar to SLA, DLP is commonly used to generate highly detailed artwork, non-functional prototypes, and can be used to make molds in investment casting applications. Main DLP 3D Printing Technologies Digital Light Processing provides excellent capabilities for 3D printing / Additive Manufacturing processes with an eye on efficiency. DLP is your go-to method when opting for a quick printing process without compromising on the quality of intricate parts. Just like their SLA counterparts, desktop DLP 3D printers are built around a resin tank with transparent bottom and a build platform that descends into a resin tank to create parts upside down, layer by layer. The difference is the light source. DLP 3D printers use a digital projector screen to flash an image of a layer across the entire platform, curing all points simultaneously.Now that you know how SLA works, it’s time to take a closer look at DLP. DLP is a “sister technology” to SLA as the only big difference is the light source used to cure the resin. As we just mentioned, SLA printers use lasers combined with galvanometers to cure resin. With a DLP 3D printer, the light source is a specially developed digital light projector screen. Thanks to this screen, DLP is generally considered to be faster than SLA, and here’s why: With SLA, the laser has to individually cure the resin in a “point to point” technique. On the other hand, a DLP projector screen flashes an image of a layer all at once! Thus all points of a layer can be cured simultaneously. In this way, the print speed is increased in comparison to SLA since it takes less time to cure a single layer. Since the DLP is a digital technology, the 2D image that is projected is composed of pixels. When translated into three dimensions, they become voxels. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) Overview Features Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview: How FDM 3D printing works? The Basics Of FDM 3D Printing Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a 3D printing technology widely known for its speed, accuracy, and competitive cost. An FDM machine precisely extrudes melted plastic filament to create a part. FDM parts can be made in as fast as one day. Benefits Of FDM 3D Printing Fused deposition modeling can build fully functional parts in standard plastics. However, they have anisotropy in the z-direction (vertical direction) and a step-structure on the surface. Fused deposition modeling works with standard materials, for instance, ABS/PA/PC. Therefore, parts have good mechanical properties and are durable over time. Parts can be post-processed as any plastic part produced with conventional manufacturing. Features of FDM 3D Printing Advantages Precision We use the most advanced industrial FDM 3D printers designed to meet tolerances of +/- 0.004” or +/- 0.002” per inch, whichever is greater. Strength FDM printed parts are available in a variety of high-performance plastics for applications that require resistance to the elements. Large Build FDM can produce FDM parts with large build volumes up to 600 x 500 x 500 mm Rapid Turnaround FDM parts do not require tooling which reduces the manufacturing lead time from weeks to days. Real Thermoplastics FDM has the highest variety of real engineered thermoplastics. Part Production FDM is capable of producing end-use parts on-demand, increasing throughput and helping you get to market faster. Drawbacks Surface Quality Extruding material layer-by-layer,the surface has layer lines and fine details cannot be realized Scale Effect The unit cost and lead time will not be reduced as much as casted or molded parts. Layer Adhesion Parts have an anisotropy in the z-direction (vertical direction), and properties are weaker than base materials. PLA PLA (FDM) is used for low-cost, non-functional prototyping. Offers greater detail than ABS, but is more brittle. Unsuitable for high temperature applications. +17 Stratasys ABS-ESD7 ABS-ESD7™ (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene-electrostatic dissipative) is an ABS thermoplastic with static dissipative properties for applications where a static charge can damage products, impair their performance or cause an explosion. ABS-ESD7 prevents a buildup of static electricity, so it will not produce a static shock or cause other materials like powders, dust and fine particles to stick to it. Ideal for electronic products with circuit boards and for the transportation and industrial equipment industries. Most widely used to create jigs and fixtures for the assembly of electronic components, but it is also useful for building functional prototypes of fuel storage and delivery products, as well as cases, enclosures and packaging. PLA-CF PLA-CF is a composite reinforcement material made by mixing carbon fiber powder into a traditional polylactic acid (PLA) plastic matrix. It is designed to retain the advantages of PLA for easy printing while significantly improving its mechanical properties. PC (Polycarbonate) PC offers accuracy, durability and stability, creating strong parts that withstand functional testing. TPU(FDM) TPU is called thermoplastic polyurethane elastomer rubber. It is a type of polymer material between rubber and plastic. It is mainly divided into polyester type and polyether type. It is a mature environmentally friendly material. TPU(FDM) 95A HF is a flexible and highly tough consumable material with excellent impact resistance. It is suitable for printing various parts that need to withstand impact, drop, and collision. PEEK PEEK is an engineering thermoplastic with excellent mechanical and thermal properties. Can be used to replace metal parts. PPS-CF PPS-CF is a carbon fiber reinforced polyphenylene sulfide composite. Thanks to the properties of polyphenylene sulfide (PPS) resin itself and the reinforcing effect of carbon fiber, PPS-CF has excellent solvent resistance, corrosion resistance, heat resistance, flame retardancy, strength, stiffness, dimensional stability, etc., and is a special engineering plastic that can meet the application needs of engineering plastics in reflushing. PETG PTEG is a very tough, durable and easy to use material. The strength of PETG makes it the material of choice for food packaging. Its natural chemical non-reactivity makes it invaluable in medical applications and is used for orthopedic and prosthetic devices. ASA ASA is a production-grade thermoplastic that can be combined with FDM technology to achieve perfect performance. ASA can build durable prototypes for fitting, shape and functional testing, or make practical end-use parts for outdoor use. Ranging from electrical equipment housings and brackets to sporting goods and car prototypes, ASA materials can make your designs more advantageous. PETG-CF PETG-CF, short for carbon fiber reinforced polyethylene terephthalate-copolyester, is a high-performance composite material made by incorporating carbon fiber filaments into a traditional PETG plastic matrix.
